speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF LETTER CARRIERS.
speechtext:
While neither the Post Office Department nor the Government has recently received any direct communication from the letter carriers themselves in reference to the matter, communications have been received from other bodies in the city of Toronto. So far as one can judge from those communications and from the newspaper despatches, the complaints appear to be based on three grounds: First, there is some complaint about the present Bill, and I am at a loss to understand what it can be, because the Bill which was passed through this House and which went to the Senate is wholly in the interests of the Civil Service employees and carries a classification which will increase salaries, dating back to the 1st of April, 1919, instead of from the 1st of April, 1920. If there is any objection to that Bill and the employees do not wish it, some millions of money would be' saved to the country if the measure were not put through. The second complaint is that the Government changed the classification. The Government has not
[The Speaker.]
of its own motion made any change whatever in the classification pertaining to the postal service. In so far as there have been any changes, they have been due to appeals made by certain classes of the postal employees against the classification as approved by Parliament. These appeals have been heard by the Board of Hearing, upon which the civil servants are themselves represented, and among their representatives is one of the trusted employees of the Post Office Department. These .appeals have been heard by the Board of Hearing and subsequently passed upon by the Civil Service Commission, and the Government has in every case approved the decision arrived at. So that if there have been any changes they have been made on the initiative of the postal employees themselves and have been recommended by the Board of Hearing, on which, as I say, the civil servants are represented. The third complaint seems to be in reference to the compensation of letter carriers. They seem to think that there should be some better compensation than that which is now provided, and I purpose giving to the House a statement of what the letter carriers will receive this year on the basis of the Bill which passed through Parliament the other day. Under the old classification the range of salaries for letter carriers ran from $626 to $939, plus allowance in respect of clothing and transportation. The new classification is $780 to 1,260, plus bonus, because the classification itself recommends that the bonus should be added. There is also allowance for clothing and transportation. Under the new classification any letter carrier who was at the maximum of his class on the 1st April, 1919, will this year receive the following pay and allowance: If he is the head of a household he will receive salary and bonus, $1,560 plus allowance, covering clothing, boots and transprotation. So that the House may appreciate what that means I will point out that each letter carrier receives a new serge suit every year, that is coat and trousers; a pair of cloth trousers every year, a cloth coat every second year, a new oivercoat every second year, and two pairs of boots every year.

subtopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF LETTER CARRIERS.
speechtext: Do the boots he gets cost nine dollars a pair?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF LETTER CARRIERS.
speechtext:
No, $8 a pair. And he receives many other articles, such as a cloth cap every second year, a felt hat every second year, a fur cap every four years, etc. He has street car transportation to and from work .and at his work. These allow-

ances for clothing and transportation to and from work constitute a substantial addition to his salary, which estimated at what they would cost him a day if he had to buy them himself would, I understand, increase his salary by over $100 per year, some would s.ay at least $150.
If a single man he will receive $1,322 salary and bonus plus the same allowance in respect of clothing, boots and transportation.
If the letter carrier has been in receipt of the maximum under the old classification for five years, and is the head of a household, his salary will be $1,656, plus allowance for clothing, boots and transportation, which considering such allowances would make his pay over 80 cents per hour's work If a single man, $1,422 plus allowance for clothing, boots and transportation.
If under the new classification he was at the minimum of his class on the first of April, 1919, and if he is the head of a household, he will receive $1,320 in salary and bonus plus allowance for clothing, boots and transportation. If a single man he will get $1,152 plus allowance for clothing, boots and transportation. These letter carriers, have (1) a forty-four-hour week (2) permanency of employment; (3) sick leave with pay and (4) three weeks holidays each year without loss of pay.

I would like to ask the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) if he is aware that the French Treaty is practically denounced and will terminate the 16th o,f this mon(h. Is he aware that the French Government is ready to extend the provisions of the Treaty until the revision of the tariff has taken place?
Rt, Hon. SIR GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce): I am aware that notice has been given for the termination of the Treaty. The term of this notice [DOT]expires on the 19th of this month, and the Treaty provisions will then become null and void.
By whom was the notice given?

Given by the Canadian Government in respect of the three months' notice. The House should know

that the French Government gave notice of the denunciation of the Treaty itself some fifteen months ago. After that an arrangement was made at the instance of the Canadian Government by which the Treaty should go on temporarily subject to three months' notice by either party to the arrangement. In view of the possible denunciation of the Treaty on three months' notice, it was not possible to carry on business because more time is required in the usual making of contracts and arrangements for the interchange of produce between the two countries. In view of the contemplated tariff legislation of this Parliament the Canadian Government decided to give notice of termination which, as I have said, will expire on the 19th of this month. The French Government has been informed that the Canadian Government is ready to take up negotiations at any time circumstances are opportune therefor.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of the Rt. Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) for the third reading of Bill No. 137, to amend the Criminal Code.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext:
Before this Bill receives its third reading I would like to- say one or two words respecting it. I was not present last night, or rather early this morning, when the measure was read a second time, and I have a few observations to make with regard to it although I realize that a large number of members-probably the large majority-will not share my views I think that generally speaking gambling in any form is regarded as a serious evil; and I want to protest- though I may have no one to support me- against this Parliament endorsing any form of gambling. I cannot for the life of me understand why gambling a few miles out
from t(he city of Ottawa should be legalized by Parliament and regarded as highly respectable while gambling on Sparks street is pronounced illegal and disreputable.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Will the hon. member please define gambling?

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Oh, it is not necessary to define gambling. My hon. friend knows what gambling is.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: That is a bad insinuation.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Everybody knows that the provisions of this Bill, No. 137, recognize and endorse a form of gambling. I am not objecting to individuals, if they so desire, indulging in betting-it would be impracticable to attempt to stop it, and I would not make any such attempt. I do not claim to be specially qualified to advocate "uplifting." But I understand that every State in the United States has made this species of gambling illegal, with the exception of two-Kentucky and one other. Michigan has prohibited it entirely; and those who desire to take part in this form of gambling instead of doing so in that State cross from Detroit to Windsor and give us the benefit of their presence there during a race meet. I simply want to protest against this Parliament recognizing and endorsing what is admitted by everybody to be a great evil. The only reason I have ever heard advanced why it should be encouraged is for the production of thorough-[DOT] bred horses in Canada.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext:
Hear, hear, that is all
right.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext:
Well, I have read the opinions of men who are experts in that line who deny that there is anything in this contention whatever. How is it that draft horses are produced in this country at a profit? Because there is a demand for them. And if there he any demand for roadsters in this country, breeders of thoroughbreds will find a market just as do the breeders of draft horses. I merely want to express my protest against this Parliament endorsing, recognizing, and legalizing this special form of gambling.
Mr. A. R. iMcMAiSTEiR (Brome): I would not like the member who has just taken his seat to feel that in the views which he has expressed he is alone in this House. I believe in fair play to all.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Freedom.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext:
Occasionally when 1
have been in the police court-

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: -in a professional capacity, which, Mr. Speaker, has not been very often, I have seen a large number of very hard looking Orientals brought before the court because they have played fan-tan.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: What is that?

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Fan-tan is a game of chance, I understand. I am not an adept in it myself but it is a gambling game.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: What about auction whist?

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: How does it work?

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext:
I cannot explain that myself, because I am not conversant with the details of the game; I will leave it to other members to fill in the details. I do not wish to detain the House unduly but I would say this:	For Parliament to enact legislation
which means that when certain classes of the community gamble they are drawn be-for.the court and fined while other members of the community may enjoy the benefits of fresh air and of gambling at the same time, is not British, is not Canadian, is not fair, and it should not be done.
Now, is it correct that the breeding of fine horses is only possible in conjunction with gambling? I have always understood that the stock-raising business was a respectable one-I believe there are members of this House who agree thoroughly with me in that, and I do not think the success of that business depends on gambling. If horseracing requires to have gambling as a concomitant we should be able to get on without it. But I do not say that because you eliminate gambling you of necessity do away with horse racing. There are some other people in Canada who are prepared to race their horses for the fun of the thing.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Did you ever own a race-horse?

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: I never owned a racehorse, and judging by the class of people whom I see coming from Tace meetings, I have no desire to own race-horses, nor to associate with those people.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: My hon. friends say "Oh, oh." Do they imply by that tone of voice that they agree with me? I say that race tracks usually draw the riff-raff and undesirable element of our own population and of outsiders. '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Horse race tracks are also frequented by a very desirable class of people no doubt. I conclude my remarks by saying that to make a criminal offence of certain types of gambling, and to recognize other types of gambling, is not fair and such 'discrimination should not be continued. I wish to raise my feeble voice in support of the words uttered by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers).

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend of the opinion that speculation on margin on the stock exchange is gambling?

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Yes, decidedly so, and a very evil form of gambling. In fact, in such gambling you do not have the benefit of the fresh air and the pleasure of seeing the horses run, and as a rule you lose your money in larger sums and with greater certainty.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext:
When I opened my morning paper to-day I noticed with great pleasure that the right hon. the Prime Alinister, when receiving a certain deputation yesterday, said that the Government had gone as far as they could along these lines. While I endorse the remarks of my two hon. (friends in regard to discrimination, I cannot do so from the .lofty moral altitude which they seem to occupy. Looking at this matter philosophically, I doubt (very much, whether it is possible to describe in such drastic terms an evil which is so widespread in human nature. A boy the moment he can own a marble risks it [DOT]against another boy's marble, and he is a gambler to that extent. If he is a better shot, he wins a marble from the other boy. There is a certain element of skill in the contest but no general good accrues to the community. I am told that the society ladies of this capital and of London play a game called auction bridge for high stakes, d never was present on such occasions and do not know anything about it from personal knowledge, any more than I know anything of the game, but I am told such things go on. Perhaps there are some hon. members here who can either contradict or *confirm this information. The other day on Epsom Downs-where I am sorry to say I have been-
Some hon. MEA1BERS: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: I am glad to say I have been-

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DISCUSSION RE RACE TRACK BETTING.
speechtext: His Alajesty the King accompanied by the Queen and

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
fifty or sixty others went to see the Derby, and I have no doubt, if I were in His Majesty's secrets, that he had a little flutter on the race. But, Sir, I come nearer home. I have not the least doubt that many of the elders who waited upon the Prime Minister yesterday are interested in real estate. I know that in the little town nearest my farm all the leading men in the churches are real estate agents, and I have been long enough in Canada to know that *something a good deal like gambling goes on in real estate offices. Then there are places called "stock exchanges" and "wheat pits,"-gambling goes on there too.
Now, from the moral point of view I want to say to my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) that the people who make money in any of these spheres of activity might just as reasonably be described as "riffraff" as the somewhat tough but nevertheless very often human beings who frequent race tracks; and with due deference to our common human nature-which in the case of any individual among us has its faults, *however well wre may succeed in hiding them-I think it would be well for us not to use such strong language, and to take the method of the Creator by going slowly in our attempts to improve human beings according to our narrow outlook. After all *the world is inhabited by a large number of different people. I am not now playing *the role of a preacher,-
Quite the opposite.

I am as a legislator talking of what it is possible for Governments and Parliaments to do; and the distinction between Governments and Parliaments and preachers is, that while preachers have the high and unapproachable role of improving human beings according to their highest ideals which is their undoubted province and duty, Governments and Parliaments have to do with all classes and conditions of men, and have to harmonize one portion of society with the other. They have perhaps the much more difficult task, and therefore they ought to go cautiously in the methods they pursue for the improvement of society. That is my view upon this question. I rose, however, merely for the purpose of endorsing what I think is the sound view, that we should not discriminate. I do not know that it will impress my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), but I am sure he would shrink at the idea of having to regulate rich companies or rich individuals, or even boys playing marbles, although he is found in
the apparently congenial sphere of activity of curbing the old-fashioned sport of horseracing. I think it wmuld be just as well to leave that sport alone.

I would like to endorse the sentiments of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). On many occasions I have in this House opposed restricting the liberties and the privileges oi the people, and I was glad to read in thi: morning's paper that the Prime Minister had had the courage to tell a deputation which waited upon him yesterday that he and his Government were not going to pass any further legislation restricting race track betting. I think our people in all classes of society are quite capable of looking after their own morals. Whether you describe them as high or low, or in the words of the hon. member for Brome describe them as "the riff-raff of the country" - which expression I do not agree with-I think they are entitled to exercise their liberties as British subjects in this country-

Canadians.
Mr. McGIBBON (Muskoka)-and they are entitled to spend their money in the way that gives them most pleasure. I am opposed to any further restrictions being placed upon the people of this country.
Hear, hear.

I think they are intelligent enough and honest enough

to conduct themselves as good free British citizens. If they do that, I think this House and the country should not ask anything further.

Mr. Speaker, Parliament settled about twelve years ago that race track gambling should not be done away with in this country. For some years afterwards there was quite an abuse of gambling at certain race tracks in this country, especially in the province of Ontario. -Several of the states on the other side of the line prohibited gambling at race tracks, and in consequence these American race track operators came over to Canada and established race tracks at Fort Erie, Windsor, and other places. These were not genuine race tracks, but simply tracks for making money for the operators. I believe this legislation will have the effect of curbing this evil, and will tend to make racing a legitimate sport instead of a mere money-making venture. I fully endorse the principle of this Bill. If you are not going to have pari-mutuels, but are going to allow people full liberty to Ibet, the gambling evil will continue and increase, because so long as New York, Michigan, and other states prohibit race track gambling, the gamblers from the United States will come over to Canada. I think the House should adopt this Bill. The consensus of opinion in this country seem-s to be against doing away with racing altogether. Horse breeders maintain that it is necessary for the -breeding of thoroughbred horses. I do not know whether they are right or not. That was a much-disputed point when the question was .raised in this House twelve years ago. I think my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Smith) would be in favour of racing, and would be of opinion that it improves the -breed of horses. He knows more about it than I do; I am not a horse breeder myself. I condemn the race track gambling evil, and I will do whatever is in my power to curb it, and as I think this Bill will have the effect of curbing it, I shall support it.

Mr. Speaker, I think this is a move in the right direction. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has stated that in the United States the great majority of the states have prohibited race track gambling, and I believe that statement is correct. Nevertheless, it is a fact that gambling at race tracks goes on to a very large extent in practically all the states of the Union. The fact is that gambling at race tracks in the United States is tolerated. An effort

is made by this legislation to bring race track gambling under some sort of control, and from what we -have seen in the United States I -believe that is a -move in the right direction. It is perfectly true that gambling at race tracks in the state of Michigan, for instance, has been stopped, but, nevertheless it is a fact that gambling at race tracks in that state is carried on week after week, and it seems to me that legislation along the lines proposed by this Bill is what we need in this Dominion in order to put the bu-siness on a proper basis.
While I do not bet at races myself, I confess that there is no sport I enjoy so thoroughly as a Tace meet, both running and trotting meets. I think it is the finest sport in the world, and should be encouraged in every country. I cannot agree with some speakers that it is a sin or something very wrong to place a bet on a horse race.
A virtuous sin.

An owner who enters his horse for a race pays his entry fee, say five per cent. If he wins the purse, he receives fifty per cent of the purse money. In other words, he bets one to ten that his horse is -going to win. Now it is a well-known fact that the men who engage in horse racing, even if they are rich, cannot maintain -stables on the purses that are given, and I cannot see anything wrong in the owner placing an additional bet through the machines or the bookmakers and in that way increasing his winnings. I should like to emphasize that point. I do not see any difference between a man paying an entry fee to win a -purse and- the man who places a -bet on an entry which he may have. The great criticism that has been made of this sport is due to the abuses that have crept into the conducting of it, and I think that to regulate this -sport, as this legislation proposes to regulate -it, is a step in the right direction. It may be that the percentages that have been struck are not quite right, but after we have had experience of them we can govern ourselves accordingly. I cannot but believe that if in this country, just as in Great Britain, we have horse racing cleanly conducted, it will work to the advantage and betterment of our people. I am strongly of the opinion that this legislation is -a move in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) prefaced his remarks by saying that he had no use for men who remarked that we were putting too^ many restrictions on people through legislation, etc. If we were to have .in Canada or anywhere else only those things and those men for Whom my hon. friend has any use, there would be ample room for them to move around, because there would be practically no one left. From



his remarks, he has apparently use for very few things, and I cannot agree with him as regards those things for which he has use.
Be that as it may, there are two classes of men in this country. First, there are men who love sport, who want their liberty and to be able to use their time three days a week or, to use the words of my hon. friend, to spend their time as they see fit for a week or two weeks. I do not see why we should put any limitations on the way a man may spend his time if he does not spend it in committting crimes, illegalities or nuisances. Who is going to prevent me from going to a club in the Laurentian mountains and sitting there-although the apparent purpose is fishing-and smoking for two or three weeks if I choose to do so, as I would be doing a perfectly legitimate thing?

The hon. member would
not be doing any good for the country.
I might be doing just as much good as the hon. member for Prescott, if he was sitting here going full speed.

I think my hon. friend
would be doing a good thing for the country by taking a rest, because then he would be fresher for next session.

The newspapers have
made an announcement that compels me to disclaim any freshness in any way you may interpret the meaning of that word. There are people who live in this country who claim the right to enjoy liberties as long as the^ are not committing crimes, nuisances or illegalities. Then there are others who think, by preventing men from following their inclinations and tastes, they are doing good for the country. I say: ' No. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) says that he enjoys a race. Very few men do not enjoy a race, but how are you going to have a race if you do not have some inducement to people to breed horses and bring them there? The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), following the argument oif the hon. member for Frontenac, says that he does not believe in racing as ian inducement to improve the breed of horses. It is the only inducement. Why do we have exhibitions, or fairs, as we call them, in every county. To get all the breeders together. Those' breeders compare notes and endeavour to improve the breed. Those fairs, bring around people who play with three shells-I do not know what the game 
is- the same as people do on race tracks. Nevertheless, you see at these fairs the best men from the farming communities.

Not "rigging the
thimble."

People get into a corner and "run the thimble" or the roulette wheel. A fair is a place where everybody in the community will go in order to get some fresh air, and at the same time to educate themselves and, perhaps, have a little fun. They are entitled to that. If I were to take any exception to this law,
I would say that it is too restrictive, and I am not ashamed to say that. At race tracks you meet as good people as you will come across, perhaps not in the police court, but in the Superior Court or in the court of King's Bench. I have never degraded nor contaminated myself by attending a good horse race; and if I lost a little money befoie I went home, I did not worry over that and I do not think anybody suffered on account of it. As regards the man who cannnot afford to bet, who is scandalised at the idea of going to a Tace track, let him stay at home. That is an easy way for him to get out of the difficulty, but why should he deprive his neighbour from a sport which I consider is just as legitimate as boxing, golfing, hockey, baseball or lacrosse?
It is cruelty to animals.

Those animals are
trained to endure things that other horses are not trained to do. I may be told that it is cruelty to a man to have him box two or three rounds. I contend that that makes him more limber; it makes him a better man, a better citizen. There is an old latin saying: "Mens Sana in corpore sano"
[DOT]-"A sound mind in a sound body." These sports contribute towards making sound bodies and sound minds. That is my view on the question.	,

Mr. Speaker, I think it requires only a short time to express one's opinion on this subject. I do not purpose fallowing the discussion which, it seems to me, has in many cases been very wide of the mark. The question is this-are we to decide that a certain thing at one time and under certain circumstances is illegal and an exactly similar thing under other circumstances is all right. I am not going to discuss the question of restriction further than to re-

peat what the hon. member for Frontenac
(Mr. Edwards) said, namely, 3 p.m. that all laws are restrictions.
That does not mean that you have to restrict a man wherever he goes, or that all restrictions are good or all bad. You must use discrimination in the restrictions you put upon people. I fail to see how we can consistently say that certain things are legal and should not be punished by fine or imprisonment if they are done in a certain place but must be punished if done in another place; that it is wrong and sinful, and therefore must be punished by fine or imprisonment for people to put up stakes in a contest of skill and endurance of persons, but that when it comes to a question of skill and endurance of animals, that is perfectly legal. Let us be consistent ; let us either allow the holding of stakes and depositing of money in all cases of this kind, or make it illegal in all cases. We are as inconsistent as it is possible for any people to be if we are to allow this in certain things and not in others.
I have not heard any good argument raised in support of the contention that gambling, if you like to use that term, or the holding of bets, which is practically what we are aiming a,t here, is necessary at race tracks in order to encourage the breeding df horses. We are told by one gentleman that it is necessary to allow the owners and breeders of horses to bet on a horse race in order that they may make some money. Does the man who Ibets on a horse race always win?
No less an authority than Sir John A. Macdonald said that there was nothing more uncertain than horse-racing and elections. This question of betting, Mr. Chairman, is exceedingly uncertain and a man who engages in it is as likely to lose as to gain. The chances are ten to one that he will lose more than he gains; and I do not see how are you going to encourage horse-racing and the breeding of horses by this measure. It seems to me that if there is any profit in this business it should be put in the way of those who breed horses. They should hold the stakes. If we are going to pass this legislation, let us be reasonable and confine the holding of stakes to the men who are breeding horses. If you.do that you will encourage horse-breeding, but not otherwise. As it is, you leave matters so that the man who is betting is on the average behind, because he must pay his percentage besides taking his chance of losing. I do not think that we can hope to promote the breeding of horses by this means. We should try to 218*
be reasonable, and this is certainly not reasonable. This Bill provides that where any person or association becomes a custodian or depository of the stakes the percentage deducted from the total amount deposited shall not exceed certain sums. Where the total amount deposited on a race is $20,000, the percentage is 7 per cent, which means $1,400, and a man is going to be the loser if he is to pay 7 per cent of the money invested. I do not think this will operate to the advantage of horse-breeders.
Rt, Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN:	This
subject has been before Parliament on many occasions within my experience, and I recall particularly a very considerable debate, after inquiry by a committee of the House, which resulted in what was known as the Miller Bill. I remember on the occasion of that discussion that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) made a very interesting and witty speech. Some hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate seem to have an entire misapprehension as to the object and purpose of this legislation. It does not recognize anything that has not been recognized for many years. The law upon the statute book as it is at present recognizes the very thing which is supposed to be recognized for the first time by this legislation. It has been on the statute and has been acted upon for fifteen or twenty years at least. Therefore when any hon. gentleman suggests that Parliament is asked to recognize something that was unlawful before, either he has not given due consideration to the subject, or he has not clearly expressed himself; because any such statement is absolutely contrary to the fact. The Government recognized, as was recognized everywhere, that there were some evils which ought to be remedied and which it might be practicable to remedy in respect of betting upon race tracks. We realized that at certain points in Canada near the frontier race meetings had been held too frequently and that large amounts of money had probably been taken out of the country. Further than that, there has been an allegation, whether true or false I do not know, that the betting at some of these places was carried on under not absolutely fair conditions. The Government did take into consideration on the one hand the necessity of restricting that evil as far as possible, and, on the other hand, of presenting to Parliament legislation that would command the assent of both Houses. I suppose that every hon. gentleman in this House will agree that it would be of very

little use for us to bring down to this House a measure that would not probably command the assent of both Houses. If it was undesirable to leave the law as it stood before, without any restriction whatever calculated to diminish the evils to which 1 have alluded, ordinary common sense would indicate that the Government would have to take into consideration first the character of the existing evils, and then the possibility of cutting them down to a minimum by legislation that would command the assent of both Houses of Parliament. At least, that is the way it struck us, whether our impression with regard to the matter was right or wrong. And what we determined to do was to impose such further restrictions upon the law already existing as would prevent unscrupulous people from coming in from abroad and engaging in this country in the practices I have mentioned. It was stated that vultures came into this country and robbed the young men of their money. Well then, the purpose of the .Minister of Jus-tic in preparing legislation was so to frame it that the evil-doers could not seize their prey, so to legislate that it would not be a paying proposition for them to conduct these meetings as they have been conducted in the past. That was the purpose and object of the legislation, and no other. It is restrictive and not enabling. It was designed by the Government from the standpoint I have already mentioned, and with the sincere desire to minimize as far as possible by legislation the serious evils to which allusion has been made. No one denies that these evils have to some extent existed. For my part, 1 share the view entertained by my colleague, the Minister of Justice, who has prepared this legislation, that it will do much to remove those evils. You cannot eradicate from human nature a certain innate desire to bet now and then and to indulge in games of chance. This desire exists in every civilized nation, and, for that matter, among uncivilized people too; and I would not be quite sure that some of the gentlemen who have spoken so eloquently this afternoon have not occasionally made a bet upon the result of an election. Well, other people desire sometimes to bet upon a horse-race, and as my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Thomson) has stated, a very eminent authority laid down the dogma in days gone by, that the result is about as uncertain in the case of an election as in the case of a horse-race. I hope that what I have said, and I have endeavoured to put the matter as plainly as I can, will indicate to the House that the purpose 
which animated the Government in the legislation was entirely in the line of minimizing as far as possible an evil that was recognized and to do so by means that would be fairly certain of attaining success.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the third time.

speechtext:
Before we proceed with the items in detail, I rise with a great sense of responsibility to ask your leave, Mr. Chairman, to make one o,r two general observations. Speaking in the presence at least of one member of this House of unrivalled experience in the matter of budgets and questions of this kind, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), I would submit to the members o.f this committee through you, Sir, that we find ourselves at this moment in a situation almost unprecedented in any British country in regard to budgets.

What is the ordinary procedure in regard to a budget? I claim, in view of the changes, in view of the tremendous alterations that are involved in the resolution, although I shall not trespass at any great length, a little latitude. The method of procedure in regard to the introduction of a budget which, in so far as I know, has been universally followed in all civilized countries, certainly in all British countries, has been that the Government brings down its budget proposals after the most careful consideration not only of the principles of the budget but o.f the machinery by which these principles are to be given effect to. The facts in regard to the principles, the details and any change in the machinery, are kept absolutely secret until the Budget is laid before Parliament. After they bring these proposals down in that way, the raising of the finances for the running of the country is so vitally important a matter that the government almost uniformly,-I will say uniformly-have taken the position : "Those are our proposals arrived at under the greatest sense of responsibility lo raise the finances for the running of the country and by those proposals substantially we stand or fall." I appeal to you, Sir, if that has not been the universal procedure in regard to the Budget.
Why has it been so? What is the reason for it? The reason is this: The secrets are kept and the Government stands or falls by its proposals because it is of vital necessity that the moment the Budget proposals are known the machinery of the Finance Department should be ready to apply them on the one hand and the business of the country should not be nearly upset on the other. That seems to me to be elementary financial history in all British countries. What have we here? I venture to think

the newspapers take this view-that we have had practically a second Budget introduced in the committee stage of these proposals. It is not an alteration in detail; it is an alteration in principle.. We have changed on a number of articles from the method of collecting the percentage on the whole price of the article to the American plan of only collecting the percentage on the excess, making an enormous difference in the amount we shall collect on any given article, this being tantamount to a change in the principles of the Budget. This is a very serious state of affairs, and I am bound to say that from my reading of the financial history of the Old Country such a state of affairs would, under ordinary circumstances, require a very drastic remedy
and would certainly call, not only for the resignation of the minister who was particularly involved, but for the resignation of the administration as well. I asked the other night what the machinery was for the collection of this tax and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance did not have any answer. He said that he might employ stamps, oblivious apparently of the precedent that is absolute that some of these taxes .were already being paid and were being collected in the imost slipshod and unprepared manner apparently because the hon. gentleman could give no description of the machinery by which he proposes to collect these taxes. The Government have been unduly firm concerning the title of their taxes under which their administration would have a second argument for interfering with the business of the country but they have been irresolute and vacillating,-and they have been attacked by the press-in regard to the vital principles of their Budget. I am very sure the minister will agree with me when I say that I have no desire on . personal grounds to see his resignation but I think the committee is entitled to full information and at once-and not only the committee but the country-first as to whether these taxes are to be immediately collected or not, because I want to tell my hon. friend the minister that from correspondence which I have had-and I have no doubt every member of this House has had-in remote districts and in near districts of the country some retail merchants are collecting the taxes-others are not. There is a beautiful state of affairs as a result of the Budget: Slipshod, haphazard, no directions. In some cases, I repeat, to my knowledge, the taxes are being collected, in some they are not; and other people are at a loss and are writing for information as to what they have got to do. The ordinary procedure in regard to Budgets is departed from just one hundred per cent in this-that absolute confusion is to be introduced into the business of the country, and the gathering of the so-called excise taxes is being carried on haphazard. .Now, we are entitled at once to information from the minister upon two points. There is this important matter, that a great deal of money has already been collected under the provisions as they were originally introduced, but those provisions are being reversed by the hon. minister himself. What is to become of the money that- has already been collected? The people have paid it; they have paid it under a law from which

the author of the law is receding. What is to come of that matter? This is a very important matter for the people that have .paid the taxes. It is a very important inat-ter for the merchants that have collected the taxes. My hon. friend will not disagree with me on terminology in this case when I say that it is a case of absolutely utter confusion and chaos.
Now, wihat the people of this country, from Halifax to Vancouver, want to know is: Are the Ministry now .so prepared to stand or fall by their .proposals that they .are prepared to give them .information as to how these taxes are to be collected, how they are to he taken care of, and what the machinery is to be; and I have no doubt that very important discussions will yet arise on that very .question of machinery. I wonder if my hon. friend has noticed-he must have noticed it, probably it has 'been brought to his close notice-that in the papers last night it was stated that the retailers of this country say that if these taxes were all collected at headquarters only nine thousand firms would be concerned. They say that collecting them in the way of sales taxes-as they ought to be called, I stick to my point-250,000 firms will -be concerned. That is the statement of the retail traders. I need scarcely point out to the committee that that statement, if it has a grain of truth in it, has a bearing of the utmost importance on the machinery that is to he used, the expense of collection, the usefulness of the taxes, and the amount of money that will be raised by it. I submit these elementary considerations; but the point I do want to impress upon the minister is that he must now have arrived at the point-which is the usual procedure, I repeat, in Budget matters-that he and the Government of which he is a member will stand or fall by their proposals, and they will give the people of this country, and the Parliament of this country, absolutely reliable and detailed information as to the machinery by which the taxes are to be put in operation.

I might say, Mr. Chairman, but of course it is really unnecessary to do so, that while the hon. member for Red Deer is very free on certain occasions with his .fulsome flattery and with his criticisms, on other occasions he is extremely sensitive to a little bit of criticism when it refers to himself. When the hon. member was endeavouring to justify the position he took at the time of his exception to the use of the word "excise," he told us and grew wonderfully eloquent-or rather somewhat boisterous-in his language that great violence had been done to the English language by the misuse of the word. I contend that the word "excise" as applied to these duties is correctly applied. These

duties are collected, in the main, on things produced and sold in Canada. I might- it will only take a moment, notwithstanding the wonderful knowledge possessed by the hon. member for Red Deer I think there is still room for him to gain a litttle information-I might just quote an authority which I do not think even he will question, even no less an authority than Adam Smith, in regard to this. Now Adam Smith says:	_
"The duties of excise are imposed chiefly upon goods of home produce destined for home consumption."
If Adam Smith had intended that the application of the words should exclusively be to goods produced in the country where they were consumed he would have left the word "chiefly" out. The use of that word by Adam Smith must mean, and can only mean, that the word "excise" while it applies generally to goods made and consumed in the country applies also to like things when imported and consumed in the country. That is an authority which I presume the hon. member for Red Deer will be disposed to accept. He will hardly charge Adam Smith with doing violence to the English language.

speechtext:
He lived a
century and a half ago.

speechtext:
Yes, that is very true. The hon. member says that Adam Smith lived a century and a half ago, but that has not prevented my hon. friend from quoting Adam Smith, as an authority, on many occasions in this House. Indeed he has not been limited by a century and a half in making his quotations; he has gone into the dim and misty ages, hundreds and hundreds of years ago, when he could quote some person-mow long since dead and gone-who had at some time in his life made use of expressions which suited the views of the hon. gentleman. In regard to this particular matter, which my hon. friend thought of sufficient importance to make the subject of an amendment to the Budget, he tells us that Adam Smith lived a century and a half ago and therefore I should not quote him as an authority. The hon. gentleman has been in this House loir twelve years, and this is the first time that he has taken occasion to move an amendment to the Budget.
Now, Sir, what has been the attitude of the hon. gentleman (Mr. M. Clark) in regard to this Budget? The Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) told hon. members with the utmost candour that he was facing a serious after-the-war situation which required the raising of large sums of money. He gave us full details of the situation, and he invited hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as well as hon. gentlemen on this side to come forward with helpful suggestions towards meeting this national difficulty. Some hon. gentlemen sitting opposite responded to that appeal. But what has been the attitude of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark)? He was not following in the footsteps of Cobden and Peel and Bright, nor was he wearing the mantle of Gladstone, when he greeted this Budget with sneers and jibes. That is the way the hon. gentleman from Red Deer met the appeal of the Minister of Finance for the assistance of all hon. members in going over these regulations with a view to amending them so that they would cause the least inconvenience to the public while at the same time providing the much needed revenue.
I have sat in this House for twelve years and have seen Budget after Budget introduced. I have seen those Budgets criticised, sometimes from the standpoint of party advantage-and we must expect a certain amount of such criticism-but never have I seen any Budget received in the manner in which this Budget has been received by the hon. member for Red Deer. What has that hon. gentleman done in the way of suggesting anything helpful? Not one single word. His whole attitude has been one of hostility, of carping criticism, of jeers and sneers and jibes, which ill becomes a gentleman who has posed for years past as a disciple of Pitt and Peel and Gladstone, and of Lord This and the Duke of That in. the Old Land, and who has offered us the benefit of his wide experience and knowledge of political affairs. Not one helpful suggestion has the hon. gentleman made, buTfrom the very beginning he has put himself in an attitude of hostility towards assisting the Minister of Finance in raising the revenue which he is honestly and sincerely desirous of raising to meet the pressing needs of this country.
I have no objection to the hon. gentleman from Red Deer expressing his views in this House. He can scatter all the flattery he likes, and follow it up by the most narrow criticism he is capable of, [DOT] but for my part I care as little for his fulsome flattery as for his blows. I ask no quarter from him; he receives none from me. But I would ask him from the standpoint of a member who has sat in this House for twelve years to throw aside politics for the
34.38

time being, and if he has any helpful criticism, to proffer it instead of offering only jibes and sneers.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to delay the committee by following my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) in all his very delicate references to myself. I rise for two purposes, and 'two only. My hon. friend has made a direct charge against me in regard to my attitude towards the Minister of Finance. He said that I had met the minister's proposals with nothing but carping citicism. I call my hon. friends attention to the fact that on the proposals for increased income tax I never opened my mouth when the Bill was going through committee, but on the second reading I did take the liberty of saying that I thought the minister might have further increased that tax. I offered no opposition except to taxes which, in the exercise of my undoubted privilege, I have my own views about. After all, I am only a human being, but I am entitled to as much respect even from the hon. member for Frontenac as God Almighty might be expected to give to a black beetle! I submit that to my hon. friend's view. That is my first object in rising.
My second object is to meet my hon. friend's quibble-because I must term it a quibble-in regard to my having quoted Adam Smith with approval on some things while not approving him on this particular thing. As a matter of fact I do approve of Adam Smith's views in this instance. I told my hon. friend and the other hon. members who listened to me on the second reading that these excise duties did exist in England 150 years ago, and I told how they were characterized at that very time by Doctor Johnston. Doctor Johnston and Adam Smith were contemporaries. I carefully guarded myself by saying further that the term "Excise Duty'' had had a precise meaning for a century. My liori. friend's complaint is that I object to taking Adam Smith, who lived 150 years ago, as an authority upon the meaning of the words current in the last 100 years, during the whole of which period he has been dead. That is the point of my hon. friend's argument.	.
I do not follow him further, because I remind myself from time to time that while a medical man in the person of Doctor Harvey discovered the circulation of the blood, n^y hon. friend has for some time held a patent for the circulation of bile.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having due regard to your ruling, and bearing in mind that we are not dealing with physiological questions, or whether some economist 150 years ago said this or that, I wish to address one or two words to the Minister of Finance on a very practical matter. May I preface my remarks by stating to the House at large that these taxes being of an entirely new character, necessarily, I think, demand from the House very careful consideration, and that where, after due thought, it is found desirable they should be modified or changed. With all due deference to my hon. friend from Red Deer, I take the stand that the hon. minister (Sir Henry Drayton) has been exceedingly wise, after hearing the criticisms from hon. gentlemen opposite and from this side of the House, and after receiving suggestions from practical men in various lines of business, to acknowledge the desirability of in some degree modifying these schedules.
I wish to make direct reference to the schedule, and before the minister-if he intends so to do-makes that definite reply so forcibly demanded by the hon. member for Red Deer, I would like the minister to consider the advisability of adding to the amended schedule hats .and caps as coming under the same category as clothing; that is, that this tax shall be levied against the amount in excess of $5, or $2, as the case may be, as against the full amount above those	two sums.
I think I make myself clear in my request to the minister. I shall now give him very briefly one or two reasons for my request.
I would like to point out first that hats can scarcely be considered a luxury until they get into a class where they are of so expensive and odd a character that the average person does not buy them. Now any felt hat under $5 is not an economical hat to buy. I am told by those who know the business thoroughly, and I had occasion some years ago to acquaint myself with this business, that it is impossible to produce under present conditions a felt hat under $5 which will be an economical

purchase, that is to say, which will bear re-shaping and cleaning, which is a very common practice amongst a great many of our citizens. Of course, you can buy a hat cheaper than that, but after a few months it is perfectly useless and cannot be re-shaped or cleaned. Upon that I base my argument that it is not desirable to discourage the purchase of let us say a $6 or $7 hat, which in the long run may be much cheaper. Now I want to make one or two direct references 'as to cost in support of this limit which I have mentioned. Upon investigation I find that the cost of the material entering into the manufacture of felt hats-and this applies also to cloth caps-has gone up anywhere from 200 to 700 per cent. This is something that is not controlled in Canada. It is not a case of some group of persons controlling this raw material and making an abnormal profit on it, because nearly all the raw material entering into the manufacture oi felt hats is imported. The same remark applies very largely to the trimmings of a felt hat. I would bring this very strongly to the attention of the minister and urge him to bring hats and caps within the same list that he has so wisely, I think, provided covering clothing. That is my direct request, and I trust the minister will give it his favourable consideration before making final answer.
Before taking my seat I would say again to the House that I think the minister has been wise in amending the schedules. As the bon. member for Bed Deer has said, we have all been deluged with requests from business people throughout this country. I have in my desk at this present moment perhaps fifty telegrams from very important business concerns in Canada, and after analysing these telegrams and considering them in the light of the amendments suggested by the minister, I find that the requests made by these gentlemen and the reasons, many of them very logical, put forward have been very largely met by the minister. So the House, I think, would be well advised to give the minister very earnest support in his effort to bring this rather difficult undertaking into proper and workable shape, rather than taking the stand, as was suggested, I believe by the hon. member for Red Deer, that the whole proposals should be swept aside and perhaps some new scheme of taxation devised. I submit that the minister has not changed the principle of his Budget, but he has very w'sely conformed to what was clearly
in the public interest in this particular form of taxation.
iMr. EULER: When the minister stated the other day that members on both sides of the House might assist him with suggestions, I had hoped that he referred not only to the various details of the taxes, but also to the method by which they should be collected. I regret very much, however, that he made it somewhat plain the other day that, so far as the method of collection was concerned, he was not disposed to make any change. I realize the difficult position in which the minister is placed in raising the necessary revenue. He has to raise a great deal of money. He is facing an unprecedented situation, and it is quite natural that in the circumstances he must adopt unprecedented, and perhaps more or less experimental means for raising the money which he has to find. He has laid down the principle that the money should largely be paid by those who can best afford to pay it, and that the taxes should be collected with as little inconvenience to the people of Canada as possible. I think it is the general opinion throughout this country that there is a great deal of money in the hands of a few people. Ordinarily we like to speak of these men as profiteers, and the general demand is that the enormous profits of the profiteers be taken from them and put in the coffers of the country. For my part, while I subscribe to that in a general way, I think there is a good deal of nonsense talked about the profiteers. I hold no brief for them at all. As a matter of fact, il believe that a great many people, including members of this House, are not profiteers, perhaps simply because they have not had the opportunity. There are many Pharisees amongst us.
The minister has adopted the plan of raising the necessary revenue largely in the form of luxury taxes and income taxes. In that way he expects to get the money from those who can beet afford to pay. Personally, I do not like very much the term "luxury taxes." I think if the luxury taxes so-called, were really luxury taxes they would very largely overlap the income tax; that is, that the men who pay the income tax would also very largely pay the luxury tax. For my part, I do not believe in calling them luxury taxes. I would call them sales taxes, or excise taxes; it does not make much difference to me which term you choose. While you may get a good deal of money from the wealthy people, I do not believe it will be possible to obtain

all the revenue that is required from that class, and I think that the plain people of this country might just as well face the fact now as later that after all the costs of this war will have to he paid by them and by nobody else, because although the wealthy man may pay in the first instance, ultimately the taxes will be passed on to the great mass of the people. If that be true, that the common people of this country will pay the great mass of the taxes, then I say let us make our method of rising the taxes just as simple and easy as possible, without trying to carry out any impossible or improbable theories. I would urge upon the minister that he do not close his mind altogether as to the best method of collecting these so-called luxury taxes, and that he do not necessarily insist now that these taxes shall be collected through the retailers of this country. I think he should take this very reasonable attitude, that the members of the committee should discuss pro and con the arguments relating to the method of collecting and then he and the Government could decide which arguments have the preponderance of logic behind them, and then let the minister adopt the best method without necessarily laying down in advance any definite rule as to how these taxes shall be collected. I do not think the minister would be stultifying himself by adopting that procedure or be necessarily called upon to resign from office, although personally I would like to see the whole Government resign. In support of my statement that he would not be stultifying himself, I say that the minister has already in effect altered some of the principles which he enunciated the other day. Reference has been made to that by other speakers. For instance, he first stated that the tax upon clothing and other articles was to be collected upon the whole purchase price, if the article exceeded a certain price.
He has now altered that attitude, and quite rightly so, in that he purposes collecting certain taxes only on amounts in excess of a certain figure. But I cannot see why the minister was not consistent in following that principle all the way through. The matter of hats has already been referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I have no particular interest in the manufacture nor in the retailing of hats; but if the minister is laying down the principle that articles of clothing shall be taxed only on certain excess values, surely hats and caps come within that category and should be

treated in exactly the same way as any other article of clothing. While food and clothing may be bare necessaries of life, it does not follow that all other things are luxuries and should, therefore, be taxable. "Man," it is said, "does not live by bread alone." Besides the bare necessaries of life such as there are, in our civilization, many things without which we cannot possibly live any sort of complete life. In our houses we need furniture, carpets, rugs, electric fixtures and many other things which may occur to the mind olf any hon. member. These things are absolutely necessary to the comfort and happiness of the Canadian people. While I admit that, after a certain point as regards prices, many of these articles take on the nature of luxuries, I contend that up to the point where they take on that nature, they should not be taxed any more than food and clothing.
I should like to examine, very briefly, the reasons upon which the minister bases his opinion that the taxes should be collected through the retailer. First, I will mention his least weighty reason, namely, that he would like to have the public realize that the war must be paid for as well as won. I do not think that is quite worthy of the minister, because the people of Canada realize in the very fullest sense that they have to pay for this war. I put that aside as an argument of no great weight.
A second argument he makes is that he has already made prices come down, and he cites instances in the city of Ottawa where prices of suits of clothes have been reduced. I have w'alked fup ,and down the streets myself, and have noticed in the windows, suits priced at $45, and in other cases at less; but jn many cases they have the magic number "45" attached to them, and he assumes that prices have been reduced from $55 or $60. I doubt whether he is justified in that assumption. I am not particularly suspicious of human nature; but 'I think our business men, retailers and others, are very shrewd, and they are apt to take advantage of almost every opportunity that presents itself. Personally, without casting any reflection [DOT]on the retailers of this or any other city, I would not be surprised if in ,some instances the prices of those suits of clothes had been actually less than $45 before the Budget was announced. The temptation is at least there, so that the argument is not very strong.
The minister advanced one argument which made some impression upon me and

which is the only one that can possibly support the method of collection which he proposes. He feared, if the tax were collected at its source, through the importer or manufacturer, the pyramiding of profits which would result all the way down from the manufacturer or importer through the jobber to the retailer, and that the actual result would be that the consumer 4 p.m. would pay more than he would if the method which the minister favours were adopted. There may he some truth in that, but the other disadvantages of the method favoured by the minister so far out-weigh the advantages of other systems which could be applied as to make it advisable to discard the method now favoured by the minister. The objection to collecting the taxes through the retailer is, I think, briefly this-the great expense, to both the Government and the merchants concerned, of making those collections. The hon. member for Oxford North (Mr. Nesbitt) stated the other day that he did not think there would be any great expense attached to this method of collection. I come from a city which has many retailers, raany merchants, and one-and all seem to think that it places upon them an enormous burden of work and care to collect that tax honestly and fairly and to pay it into the treasury. The minister also stated that, as regards cost of collection to the Government, he did not purpose going to any great expense; that he thought he could trust the retailers to make their returns honestly and fairly. I am not going to take any great issue with that statement; but the minister has lived long enough to know that there is no class of people in Canada, nor probably in any other portion of the world, who willingly pay taxes, I do not care how patriotic those people may be. Those of us who know anything with regard to statements made in connection with the income tax, know there are very few men who deliberately pay that income tax except as they know they must pay it. Perhaps I am wrong in that; perhaps I am misjudging human nature; hut I believe I am right in saying that, as a general principle, people will not willingly pay taxes, no matter what the form of those taxes may be nor for what purpose they may be imposed, and if the Government wishes to get the tax, it must adopt some means of seeing that it actually receives that which it expects to receive. I believe in many cases the merchants will not collect all the taxes, nor will the Government receive the taxes
collected in all instances. In all this I am making no reflection upon the retailers as a whole.
- Again, there is so much lack of information on the part oif the people and on the part of some of the merchants as to commodities upon which these taxes shall be applied, that, in many instances, taxes will be collected from people entirely illegally because the commodities on which those taxes are collected are not 'taxable at all. I happened to hear yesterday of an incident which illustrates that point. A traveller who came from the city of Montreal went into a confectionery store in order to buy a box of candy priced at $1 or $1.20, and the retailer insisted on collecting from that man what he called a luxury tax, although the collection of it was not legal. I am afraid a great deal of that sort of thing will occur. Further, even if this method of taxation might be in the interest of a large mass of the people, it is not fair to put one section of the public, such as the merchants, to all the inconvenience and expense consequent upon this method of collection.
The other method of collection suggested is that the 'tax be collected at its source from the manufacturer or importer. If the minister decided to adopt that' plan, he would not 'be violating any principle already laid down by him, because, as a matter of fact, he has already adopted'that plan in other instances. I for one do not believe musical instruments, pianos, phonographs, are entirely luxuries. In the case of musical instruments the minister is collecting from the manufacturer; (the retailer of musical instruments does not. collect the luxury tax as such at all. If the principle be right in the one case, I am at a loss to understand why a departure is made from it in another case. Therefore, it would not involve any departure from a principle laid down by the minister if he desired to adopt one principle and observe it all the way through. If that method is adopted, he can simplify the -whole process to almost as great a degree as possible. Every manufacturer, every importer, every wholesaler, in fact every merchant, if he does his business in an up-to-date way, keeps a sales book or at least has some record of his sales, and it is the easiest matter, at the end of every two weeks or every month, to ascertain exactly what the sales have been and then calculate the tax upon them. And if the Government desires to verify the returns it is a much more simple way than to go from retail store to retail

store and search through thousands, and indeed hundreds of thousands, of sales slips which the merchants are expected to keep. In addition to that, I contend that the tax will not be felt as a tax. I maintain that the manufacturer or the importer will merely add that tax to his overhead expenses the same as any other overhead expense, and it will be absorbed into the general costs of doing business.
I rose to make one other suggestion and I am rather surprised that it has not been made before. Another method of collecting this tax has been suggested in the press and in discussions of this matter, but I have not yet heard it made in the House. In passing, I may say that I prefer the method just mentioned. But if the minister has objections to collecting the tax from the wholesaler or the manufacturer at the source of production because of a fear that the consumer will pay more, then I would ask him to consider the suggestion that the tax be collected upon the entire sales of the retailer as well as those now paid by importer and manufacturer. That method will have almost all the merits and advantages of collection through the manufacturer and importer. The books are there and the sales are shown, and there will be very little inconvenience and expense either to the retailers or the Government in making the collection, while it will remove the dangers which the minister sees in the pyramiding of profits all the way down from the importer or manufacturer to the retailer. The retailer will simply add the one per cent, or whatever the percentage may be, to his overhead, and it goes out to the consumer with very little added cost as compared wdth the method proposed to be used by the minister. You would, I believe, obtain almost exactly the same amount of money by employing that method of collection as by the present method, and with much less inconvenience. A retailer of this province who has been carefully collecting the tax for a period of ten days under the present system found that- during those ten days the sales amounted to something like $4,400, or $4,300 and that the luxury tax amounted to exactly $43. That is just as close to one per cent of the total sales, as you could arrive at, and I make the deduction from that that if that method were adopted of placing a tax of one per cent on all sales, except foods, you would obtain just about the same amount of revenue as if you adopted the method proposed. I do submit that it would be much simpler, would cost a great deal less and would be less inconvenient. I make this

suggestion for the consideration of the minister, and as I said on rising, I hope he has not made up his mind firmly to adhere to his other plan. I simply want to see the money obtained in the least burdensome manner, and with the least amount of inconvenience to the public and expense to the Government. .

speechtext: What the hon. gentleman has just read is the exact definition of an excise tax if I understand it. It was an excise duty imposed on goods manufactured in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has a way of listening with one ear and closing the other. He has a way of shutting his ear when the argument is against him just in the same way as he sometimes clouds and closes his intellect when the argument is against him for in the very preceding sentence I read, exactly the opposite thing was done. The excise was put plainly, straightly and strictly upon the imported article and not only on the imported article but on the value of the imported article duty paid. The point really is too plain to labour, and I only labour it because I have the greatest respect for my hon. friend and I am sure he was sincere in the first instance when he

approached this subject. But he sees how the taxes are described in. this Act. If further light were required I would invite him to consider the automobile tax. If he looks at that tax he will find that it ia called an excise tax equal to ten per cent of the duty paid value of the imported article or equal to the manufactured cost if manufactured at home. I know my hon. friend always understood that there was no tea grown in Canada and that the excise tax on tea was certainly a tax on an imported article. That is what he called it when he voted for an excise tax. I refer him to the section dealing with the tax on tea. He will find the same thing in regard to cinematographs and other things. The thing is really, too plain, too clear, for further argument. It is a quibble that is unworthy of my hon. friend.
There is one other ground advanced by my hon. friend. He says that not only in the first instance did I shatter the English language, the dictionary and everything else but that to-day I am absolutely shattering and ruining all proper parliamentary procedure.
On the subject of parliamentary procedure I yield with the greatest deference to my hon. friend I do not know much about parliamentary procedure but I had hoped that when I came into this House I [DOT]was going to learn a great deal about it from my hon. friend. One of the things I am suffering from at the present time is the greatest sense of disappointment because I know my hon. friend could give me that instruction, I know that he knows the subject well, but again I am afraid that my hon. friend was not entirely sincere in the manner in which he approached the point. For example, he appealed in connection with the Budget debate, or rather in connection with the point he was making, to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) for help, for assistance and for light. Well, of course, it was not forthcoming. Why? Because the very thing that is being done to-day was done in this House in November 1896. It is no new thing to change Budget resolutions in Parliament. It is no new thing to change the duties when taxes have gone into effect. It is no new thing, after all, to try-never mind at what minute you attempt it-to try and do the right thing, and it was done in November 1896. Why, the tariff was introduced by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, when he was Minister of Finance, in November of 1896. It wa.s approved in March

1897; and there the same question came up, that has to come up here when changes are being made. For what reason? In the public interest and to make the scheme of taxation proposed a better scheme, changes were there also made. In that case the section respecting the date of rates going into force provided that in cases where rates were reduced-and rates ivere reduced with the Government staying in office, as my hon. friend knows very well-refunds would be made dating back to November while increases-and increases were then made after the Budget had been introduced -only came into effect on the date the resolutions were adopted in March. So, Mr. Chairman, as far as the precedents of this House are concerned at any rate, what we are doing at the present moment is covered by precedent.
There is really one claim made by the hon. gentleman, and it is that the Government should come down to the House with an adamant face, shove their proposals through with the force of their majority irrespective of those merits which arguments and discussions here may substantiate. After all, the Government's responsibility is of such a character that in order to do the right thing and the honest thing the tax in the first instance can only be considered, as the hori. gentleman well knows, privately and without the intimate knowledge-under our methods of Parliamentary procedure-the intimate knowledge that an inquiry would give. Notwithstanding that, notwithstanding that an error may be made, in the opinion of my hon. friend there must be no change in the Budget but it must be forced through whether it be in the public interest or not. Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not know what the House thinks of that as a principle, but it would seem to m'e to be a very extraordinary one. I should have thought that no matter what legislation may foe introduced, it can be improved by discussion in the House and that unless measures are to be improved here from time to time there is not an awful lot of justification in having a House. It seems to me to be most extraordinary that the silver-tongued orator of democracy-who preaches democracy in the highways and the byways-does not, after all, understand its meaning, and that that silver-tongued apostle of democracy has today become the brazen-mouthed trumpet of absolutism and autocracy.
