This is not an academy, and it seems to me we have gone far afield

this afternoon to define a word the meaning of which has been practically decided a day or so ago. I wish to call the attention of the committee, in a few brief sentences to another aspect of the case, and I invite the attention of the Finance Minister to the amendment I am about to move. Let me say at once that I have received several letters and resolutions bearing on this subject. Personally I am quite ready to do my share to help this country to carry on. I have already formulated my objections to my hon. friend's resolutions. I consider that his taxes on luxuries are more or less taxes on necessities; but on this point we expressed our respective opinions when the Budget Speech was delivered and in the discussion which followed. I have no doubt that the House and the country will have to face the passing of these resolutions with their attendant consequences, although from now on perhaps a few amendments may be made. For my part I repeat that I am ready to face the situation, to help the country to carry on, provided my hon. friend will amend his resolutions so as to give a living chance to the poor man, and see that at least the necessities of life are not made taxable.	[DOT]
But I am rising this afternoon with a different object in view. As I stated a moment ago I have received several resolutions and letters bearing on the amendment which I intend to offer. When our boys left for the front, they left with the blessings of their parents, and also with the solemn promise made by Parliament and by Canada as a whole that their dependents would be eared for and that they themselves, if they returned, would be cared for by the country. In my humble judgment, no country in the world did as well as Canada for the dependents of the soldiers during their absence at the front. The Patriotic Fund, the Red Cross Society and the va'rious private organizations in the country, did fairly well by the dependents of our soldiers during the time the latter were at the front. But the soldiers have returned-at least the majority of them have-and in the case of those who have not returned and will never return the country has been providing for their families. Has the country provided in an adequate manner for those families? This is not the time to say. Speaking of those who have returned to Canada, speaking of those who constitute the Great War Veterans, there has been, I am bound to say, a sad experience. They have been refused by the Government the gratuity which in other countries has been paid to returned soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
May I ask my hon. friend a question? I would very much like information regarding those other countries to .which he refers, and the amounts of the gratuities they granted to their returned men.
IMr. LEIMIEUX:	I am not saying that
this country has not done something for its returned soldiers. But as regards gratuities paid by some other countries, I will be able at a later stage to give my hon. friend full particulars. It is quite possible that Canada was not in a financial position to give the returned soldiers all that they demanded. I remember a very forcible statement made by my hon. friend's predecessor (Sir Thomas White) before a Select Committee of this House, and I am bound to accept it as an accurate statement of the case. However, I state the plain, bald fact that our returned soldiers, who had been promised that they would be cared for on their return, were refused the gratuity they asked from the Government.
But this is not the most serious difficulty which faces those men. On their return they are confronted with the extremely high cost of living. While this is very serious for the ordinary citizen, I claim that it is far worse for the returned soldier, for the former has not had his nervous energy depleted nor his earning capacity impaired; but the latter is not yet himself again. It will take the returned soldier who spent five, four, three or even two years at the front many years, before he regains his normal state of health, although he may not have been wounded. I invite the attention of the doctors who sit in this House as to the correctness of my statement.
It is true that Parliament has done something to help the returned soldier re-establish himself in civil life by giving him the benefit of vocational training; but still he is not on a footing of equality with his neighbour who remained at home to face the struggle for existence. It will be generally admitted, I believe, that the most difficult period for the returned man is this very period of re-establishment, for he has practically to start life afresh. Generally he is blessed with a family, and with the present high cost of living and handicapped by his impaired vitality, he finds himself unable to stand the strain of the economic struggle.
Therefore with the new Budget resolutions materially adding to the burdens of the tax payer, I appeal to my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) to extend to the sol-

dier and to his dependents the hand of fellowship,-to be generous and at the same time to be grateful to the returned soldier. But my hon. friend will ask me: How can we create an exception? The law of the land must apply to every person, and the returned soldier should not be exempt from its operation. My answer, Mr. Chairman, is very simple. And let not my hon. friend believe for one moment that I am appealing to popular passion in what I am about to state; on the contrary, I am trying to help him. Yes, the law of the land must be applicable to every citizen and no one should claim exemption from its operation. Yet may I remined my hon. friend that during the war, while the soldier was at the front ready "to go over the top," to give his all for his country and for the great principles of democracy, under the stimulus of the most ardent patriotism, yet at home, when asking the people to fill the Treasury with their savings, the Government was giving to a special class of the community exemption from taxation. Loans were floated at a very high figure, and those loans, known as "Victory Loans," representing immense sums of money, mostly profits made out of the war, were issued with a special label "exempt from taxation." To-day I know of some war profiteers and of some very wealthy men, patriots at large, who have invested, and rightfully so, their savings and profits in those loans, and who are therefore absolutely exempt from taxation. Let me say, en passant, to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that if there is one thing which has thrilled this country, it was his first administrative act of last fall when in his drive for the last Canadian domestic loan he refused to exempt the bonds from taxation. I give this credit to my hon. friend:	He was hold
and patriotic when he took that firm stand, which was in strong contrast with the stand taken by his immediate predecessor. We have been told that this country was intensely patriotic during the war. Well, Sir, as an evidence of our patriotism during the war let us never mention the Victory loans, except the last one, which was launched after the war, and which showed the loftier spirit and the nobler instincts of the Canadian people. All honour to my hon. friend. I have given him an example, and I have given him a precedent, the exemption from taxation of the Victory loans issued during the war when our boys were at the front exposing their lives. I say to my hon. friend that the returned soldier and his dependents will have to pay part of the

price of the enormous advantages secured by the bonded aristocracy of Canada. The high cost of living may be assigned to various causes, but I am quite sure that one of them is the fact that so many millions and millions of dollars invested in Victory loans are to-day exempt from taxation and do not yield a red cent to the needs of the country. As a Tesult the returned soldier after exposing his life at the front, finds when he returns to this fair land of his and ours that he has to pay for the financial blunders of my hon. friend's predecessor. Would you allay the feeling of unrest which exists among the soldiers? Would you prevent sedition? Would you call a halt to any unhealthy agitation in Canada? Would you put an end to this claim for a gratuity which the country cannot afford to pay? If you would, I can suggest a remedy to my hon. friend at once. I can assure him that the returned soldiers will as>k no favours from the Government in the way of exemption from ordinary customs duties and the other taxation burdens which Canada has imposed upon her children, but as my hon. friend is to-day asking Parliament to endorse a resolution which in his own words is temporary, and preeminently an after-the-war measure to meet a war contingency, I say to him, let the soldier and his dependents be exempt from the taxation which you are imposing by this measure. Mr. Chairman, the churches of this country are exempt from taxation on certain articles which they import for use in divine service. The Government accedes to the request of the churches because it respects the object which the churches have at heart-the morality, the Christianization and' generally the uplifting of the people. But patriotism is also a religion, and I believe there is no higher form of patriotism than the one which was exemplified on the battlefield by our soldiers.
I conclude my brief remarks in order to bring forth from the lips of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance an acquiescence to the principle of my amendment because he is too good a patriot himself not to stand, by the returned soldier. I therefore beg to move to amend the present resolution by inserting after the word "that" in the first line of the first paragraph the following words:
-except in the case of returned soldiers who have seen active service overseas and their dependents who shall be exempted from the said taxes for a period of five years from the date of

the sanction of the Act to be based upon the present resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I do not know at the moment whether an amendment of that kind is in order, but I should not like to raise any question of order on a matter relating to the returned soldier. I can tell my hon. friend at once that of all His Majesty's subjects who could have any claim to exemption the claim of the returned soldier is greater than all the others put together and multiplied many times over. It is just a question how the returned soldier should be helped. It is just a question how he can best be helped. It is just a question whether or not-and this is a matter which has had attentive and anxious consideration-the returned soldier would like to be placed in a special class having regard to hi9 purchases to the amount of a few dollars in the half year and to the amount of not many dollars in the whole year. It is a question whether he would rather not be put in that class of. taxdodgers or something else. Would he not rather that the country should obtain as much revenue as possible even although he paid $1 or $2, yes, perhaps, $10 a year in luxury taxes? After all, what do these luxury taxes amount to? Would he not sooner pay, perhaps, $25 or $30 a year in order that the country should obtain as much revenue as possible? !It may well be that this returned soldier would say: ''I, who am in a position to pay, would rather pay my honest share so that my country may be in a position to help my less favoured comrade to have just a little bit more for pensions, yes, that my country may have a little bit more for the disabled man and for the widow of my fallen comrade."
I do not want to treat the returned soldier question in any slushy way, and by a pretence of helping him with a small exemption, to seek to curry favour, and so far as I can see, that is what I would be doing, if I were to do as is suggested. This matter is receiving very careful consideration; and if we give the returned soldier any exemption, 'I am inclined to think we should not do it in connection with a few luxury taxes, as the amount of exemption would be of little consequence in comparison with the sacrifices the returned soldier has made, but we should, perhaps, do something larger and bigger, maybe by giving the returned soldieT absolute exemption on income. That whole question, however, is in the hands of a very capable committee. I hasten to 219
assure my hon. friend that any feasible suggestion he can make as regards exemption which will really amount to something will be taken into consideration. We cannot, however, consider suggestions which, if put into effect, might be taken advantage of by traders who were not honest, because after all, how could you check the shops? When I considered this matter, the point that bothered me was this. Here is a shop which happens to foe the black sheep in the hundred. In that shop the merchant has sold goods on which luxury taxes ought to have been paid; but he says: I sold that to returned soldier So-and-so, and I sold this to returned soldier So-and-so, and the effect would be that you would not be giving exemption to the returned soldier, but, to a very large extent, you would be putting the dishonest trader in a position where he could exact the tax and, having exacted the tax, could put it into his pocket. That is the difficulty. There is no trouble at all about meeting my hon. friend on the question of what one can do for the soldier. We cannot do too much for him within the ability of the country to do and to pay.
Just one other thought. I would suggest to my hon. friend, in a spirit of the greatest kindness-should we not, for the time being, stop worrying about what |was done during the war? That is done. Why say that Sir Thomas White was the only man in the world who ever sold tax-exempt bonds when tax-exempt bonds issued in the United States make the issue of tax-exempt bonds by Sir Thomas White look as absolutely nothing. Moreover, the statement was made in this House only yesterday that one lof the reasons for trouble in this country was that the Government had surrounded themselves with a favoured few to whom they had given tax-free bonds. Of course, if that statement had not been made in this House, one would wonder very much where the gentleman who made it came from and what his mentality was. But the hon.
member for Maisonneuve and 5 p.m. Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) should remember that every citizen, every white man left in the country, formed part of that band that is described as the band supplied with ,bonds, everybody from the highest to the lowest, from the poor man who could afford, out of his savings for the whole year, to buy only a little fifty dollar bond, up to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. No more effective appeal was made, no nobler sentences were penned than those of the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid



Laurier *when he asked his fellow countrymen to do their duty by subscribing to these bonds, thus becoming a part of the Governmental favoured few as described in this House yesterday. Everybody was in it; everybody was then doing as he thought best for Canada. Not a Canadian newspaper, worthy of the naane, was not dedicating space to this appeal to buy bonds. When we are all in it, is it not time that vre should stop quarrelling pbout it? Moreover, those bonds may be very readily obtained in the market at the present time, and although they are free of taxation, they may in some instances be bought today at less than par. That of itself is surely a sufficient answer. But the soldier's case does not rest upon that rope of sand suggested to support it; the soldier's case is such that, on his own merits, we in this House ought to do everything we can for him.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
There are
three grounds on which I find at the present time that I cannot support the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) although, perhaps, he may be able to remove my difficulties. It would be an act of supererogation to profess sympathy for the returned soldier. I take it that every man in this House has sympathy for him. But the first objection I see to my hon. friend's amendment is that some returned soldiers are excellently well able to pay these taxes, and not only would they be excellently well able, but, as the minister has said, they would be very willing to pay them. How would my hon. friend proceed in a case of this sort? Would he exonerate those men whether they were willing and able to pay or not? That is a practical difficulty of great importance. The second point, which seems to me to be also of practical importance, is that there would be a very large opening for fraud. The practical difficulty of collecting which applies to these taxes generally and all around, would be intensified in this particular case; you would need to go around the country marking your returned soldier, and every retail salesman would have to have the mark. That is only incidental to the third difficulty. My third difficulty in regard to voting for this particular amendment is that if I voted for an amendment in favour of exempting somebody from this tax, I am afraid I would be misunderstood as being in favour of the taxes generally, and I want still, in spite of all that has 
fallen from the minister, to say that I am entirely unrepentant upon that point.
I think I shall be speaking within the bounds of the amendment if I take just a minute or two to pay some little return attentions to my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) in regard to the remarks he devoted to me a few minutes ago. He started out with an assurance which I wa.s very glad to receive, that he did not take my opposition to these taxes as a personal thing. I am bound to say that his manner did not agree with his words, because I was rather glad, when he was getting back at me, that a couple of benches were between us for he seemed to be almost on the point of making a pounce upon me. We shall however, rub out his manner and accept his words. I was surprised to hear from the minister that I was ploughing a lone furrow in regard to my opposition to these taxes. I had an /dea that he had been receiving deputations night and day on this subject. If I am ploughing a lone furrow in this House there are plenty in the furrow outside, as my hon. friend knows very well. One of his followers told us that he had under his hand some fifty telegrams of protest at the time he was speaking.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The hon. member is
hardly correct. I said I had about fifty telegrams suggesting changes and improvements which I commended to the consideration of the minister.

If they want

They want to make a
good thing better.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Now, in regard to the question of direct taxation, my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) has charged me with inconsistency. Let me say that I have been in favour of direct taxation, but " direct " is not the only word to qualify a good tax. I never said I was in favour of direct taxation without regard to its incidence, its ease or its difficulty of collection, and a number of other considerations. Directness is not the only quality we must consider in a tax. There are two other qualities that occur to my mind as given by Adam Smith, and he has never been contradicted in regard to them. The first point is that a tax ought to be levied, as far as possible, in proportion to the ability of the people to pay them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
That is why
Germany and the United States followed the example of Sir Robert Peel and Mr. Gladstone in finding the easiest method of collecting direct taxes in the shape of income taxation. But a greater than Germany, a greater than the United States, a greater than Peel and Gladstone is here and says he discards the income tax, and introduces a lot of brand new things in the shape of sales taxes, although he evidently does not know exactly how he is to get them, because he forgot, before he sat down, to answer the most practical question I put to him as to how he was going to deal with those who had already paid, and how he would collect the taxes that remained. He does not answer the practical questions, which after all are all-important in the committee stage of business. Another elementary quality of good taxes is that, in addition to being direct, they should be easy of collection. That is another of Adam Smith's cardinal principles, and as my hon. friend has asked me for some lessons in political economy he is welcome to these primer suggestions in that direction. Has my hon. friend found this tax easy of collection up to now? The great majority of the people concerned want to prevent him from starting to collect them at all. .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will have ample opportunity of expressing his opinions: we are in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I simply desire to say that they are not easy of collection. They are almost as difficult as the income tax, and I only hope they will not be as bad.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has a short experience of the collection of income tax. After all, it has been found in those countries I have mentioned that the income tax is at any rate absolutely certain and well defined in its incidence, and that is also a point to be considered in a good tax. About the incidence of these taxes there is no certainty whatever; if a man does not buy he does not pay. He avoids taxation altogether, and there are a number of people who are taking full advantage of that avenue of escape at the present moment. But let me draw the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that if he took the advice offered to him by the hon. member for East Elgin and sharply graded the income tax up from the minimum, 219*
gradually grading down the sum at which he collected the tax, its incidence would be absolutely fair. And if he- will condescend to learn something from the countries that have been imposing income tax for generations he will find that it is vastly easier to collect than this tax. I am glad to have the admission that my hon. friend does not find these taxes easy of collection.
Now, I have met his main point, and the only other point I want to meet is one in which his argument was shared by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister the other night. The thing that rather bothered me in the discussion, which I am reluctant to revive, is the contention, in support of the title, that it had been allowed to escape the notice of Parliament two years ago. Well, I would say to both my hon,. friends that they do not go far back for their precedents, and if we made a mistake on a small scale two years ago that would hardly be a reason for continuing it upon the present scale of magnitude. For one thing, I have not a very great deal of respect for precedents set by this Parliament. Perhaps my right hon. friend and his colleagues would like me to tell them why. Well, if this Parliament only gets time enough it runs away from its own precedents, and so does the Government. The Government, in the person of 'the ' Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), introduced a resolution in favour of daylight saving and carried that measure almost nem. con. There were a few voices crying in the wilderness in protest against it, tout my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was not then in the House. There were some of us who told the Government that they were getting into a sea of trouble over the matter, but they paid no attention to us. They never heed any warning until they are in trouble, and they therefore disregarded the representations that were made to them. The next year, what does this Parliament do, the Parliament that I am asked to accept as one entitled to set precedents? Parliament, by a vote of two to one, rubs out its almost unanimous- vote of the year before; and I think I am therefore giving a good reason why I should not accept with any great heartiness precedents set toy this Parliament, especially precedents of such recent origin as two years ago, in contradistinction to the well-established practice and knowledge of the last hundred years. My hon. friend was not in Parliament, but he was a handy man at the -time. Of course, he was chairman of the Railway Commission, and the real fact of the matter was that neither Parliament nor the

Government hid anything to do with the setting of the time of the country. It was being set by the railways of the United States. When it was necessary to have a precedent in this matter the hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) changed the time. Now, clearly when the first law was established it must have been a federal law, otherwise so old a parliamentarian as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce would never have introduced the measure and commended it to Parliament. But when the United States railways ruled in a contrary way, my hon. friend comes down, and he says to Parliament: "This is all wrong. The precedent of Parliament and of the Government is all wrong. This is a municipal matter, and you had better rub out last year's doings and proceed differently this year." And now we are proceeding two ways and Parliament is having nothing to say about it. The municipality stands on one side, the railway stands on the other. Parliament stands in the middle of the Pleiads, looking at one clock and at the other, while the Government says: "You are in the middle; you pay your money and take your choioe." I hope I have given my hon. friend sufficient reason why I have not a great deal of respect for his precedents. I do not want to renew the argument upon this question of title, nor do I desire to hold up these taxes. I do not want to be misunderstood. I understand the responsibilities of the Government,, but a 'certain amount of parliamentary criticism is proper, and no man of the courage of my hon. friend resents it. He is able to retort in fair good style, and if he had a good case he would	be a	first-rate debater.
He will find it is a great help to his debating powers to get his case as good as he can but I am afraid that before this thing is through he will find that his case is a very bad one. I do not want to hold this up. My hon. friend displayed some little heat. I like a man to be able to get mad once in a while even in Parliament. You remember that the Scriptures say "Be angry and sin not". But I do not like a debater to be so forgetful that he does not think of answering a practical question. I want to know what is to become of the taxes that already have been collected under his first method of procedure because I apprehend he is not going to stick to the money and keep the rest of it as well. Could he give us any idea of how far he will accede to the appeal which I have made, supplemented by my hon.

friend from Waterloo (Mr. Euler), and which I dare say will come from other parts of the House? Is he disposed to respond to the appeal that these taxes shall be collected at the centre instead of from the retailers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I must confess that I find it altogether difficult not to answer the appeal made by my hon. friend. I think he really wants an answer this time. I thought before that he did not. I thought before that he was not very anxious to get an answer. Perhaps I should not speak for the Government because we have not had a chance for consultation over this question which has been brought up, but personally, I am not convinced that the method proposed is not the right one. Personally, I am not convinced that our first duty is not to the customer in the shop, to the ultimate consumer rather than to the gentlemen who are in business. Personally, my feeling is that we should leave the end of the string just where we leave it whether, as my hon. friend says, the tax may or may not be paid. Just where we leave it so that the customer has the right to make an extravagant purchase if he pleases, just where we leave it so that the full incidence of the tax will fall where we believe it will fall and there is no doubt where it falls and who is paying it, and just where we leave it so that it is impossible for the merchant to make a profit on the tax. I am perfectly free to admit that the method which we propose is the easier. It is a question whether the Government should consider ease of administration, its own comfort-yes, more than that, its own popularity It is a question whether it should consider its own popularity or whether it should consider the needs of the people and the necessity of doing everything it can to reduce cost. I know these taxes are very unpopular but I never took up the position of Finance Minister with any idea that I could be popular and at the same time act decently towards the country. I know I am making enemies every day, but I care not how many I make if I can do. anything in my humble way towards pulling down costs, bettering conditions and advancing the welfare of Canada. After all is not the sense that one has done his duty to his country really better than popularity gained by doing otherwise? I do not pretend to know it all. I have been greatly impressed by a number

of the ^remarks which have been made. As to the collection of these taxes, we have the Department of Inland Revenue with offices to collect them all over the country. The Department of Inland Revenue will look after the collection of these taxes. The ordinary way of collecting a tax of this kind would be to treat it just the same as we treat the excise tax which manufacturers have to pay and as we treat the excise tax collected from the people that are selling whiskey. We would get from them a monthly or a bi-monthly statement. It is not suggested that the statement should cover all the sales. That statement should only caver transactions involving the payment of the tax. That would be the ordinary way of collecting the tax. It is certainly true that we would have to engage more people-a lot more people-there is no doubt about that. There is that objection to it. There is another way that is being considered to see how it would work out practically and which, if possible, would do away with the accounting question, and that is by using stamps. The merchant would have to have stamps on hand and an arrangement could be made by which he could buy them readily at the post office at any time. These stamps would have to be affixed to the Bill and cancelled. Whether that will be done I really at the moment could not definitely say but that in brief will be the method under which these taxes will be collected.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
With a view to helping my hon. friend on that question of stamps may I remind him that we have been collecting taxes by stamps and he himself is making an alteration in the case of drugs because of the difficulty he has had in getting the money. I heard of a case the other day where a retail druggist got $10 worth of stamps at the beginning of the imposition of this tax and he showed them to a man in his drawer still unused, the result being that the Government got nothing. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred druggists forget to put the stamp on. If the retailers are going to forget to put the stamps an to anything like the same extent the minister is not going to get as much money out of this tax as he expects.
'In regard to his courage and determination to be unpopular, let me remind him that Mr. Gladstone once said that a Chancellor of the Exchequer who was not prepared to face unpopularity in the discharge
of his duty is not worth his salt becaus* he is the custodian of the public finances and his first consideration ought to be the public good. But, in my hon. friend's ex-_ traordinary desire to be unpopular, which is somewhat abnormal amongst politicians, he should not lose sight of the necessity of getting an easy method of collecting the tax-or rather not easy but inexpensive. That is his first duty. In spite of his intense desire to be unpopular he must get the most money he can for the Government at the least possible expense.

speechtext: This exchange of opinions between the hon. member far Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is very interesting indeed but I must remind the committee that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has been entirely lost sight of. The Finance Minister proposes changes in the taxation in connection with the boot and shoe trade, the tailoring trade, ladies' wearing apparel and other trades. He proposes to do that by taxing the excess over a certain amount-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: While this amendment may appeal to many members,,and to many people throughout the country I do not think it will appeal to the majority of Canadians as a whole. We are prepared to assist the returned soldiers in every way that we can, and we have gone a long distance in that direction. In fact I think this Government has been more than generous in assisting the returned soldiers and their dependents in many ways. But when it is necessary to raise a revenue for the purpose of carrying on the business of the country, and to assist in its development, it is a question whether to grant and exemption, which will be so far-reaching in its scope, is the proper thing to do. Members have not had time to carefully consider whether they should support this amendment or not. On the face of it, however, it does not seem reasonable that we could accord the amendment support when it will have such far-reaching effect upon the revenue that we are trying to raise. I am afraid this amendment would deprive us of almost fifty per cent of the revenue that we are aiming at, and we would have to make up that deficiency from other sources. Therefore I do not think it would be in the best interest of the country to support an amendment of such a nature at this time. At the same time we all sympathize with its objects and if the financial position of the country warranted us in granting this exemption we would all be delighted to do it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I do not propose to enter upon an academic discussion of the principles of the Budget, or indeed to participate in the pleasing discussion which took place between the Minister of Finance and the member for Red Deer, but will confine myself to the amendment before the committee. There is no need, as the hon. member for Red Deer very correctly said, for any one to protest against the proposition when his sympathies are with the returned soldier and his dependents. But the amendment of the hon. member is altogether impracticable; in actual working out it would prove quite impossible. I remember very well a practice which at one time obtained in the retail trade of this country that 
will serve to illustrate the difficulties which would attend the operation of such a proposition. The practice in question was to give a special discount to certain privileged classes in the community. The retailers accorded a discount of ten per cent to dressmakers, to clergymen, to charitable institutions, and to the clerks in all the retail stores. Even had the privilege stopped there it would not, perhaps, have been an unmixed blessing. But unfortunately the dressmaker and her friends and her friends' friends obtained the discount and the same thing happened in the case of all the other classes who enjoyed the privilege. From my own personal experience I figured that ninety-five per cent of the retailers' customers enjoyed the privilege while the remaining five per cent, who lined up and paid the full price of their purchases and never obtained the discount, were discriminated against. The practice was discontinued and now no special favours of this kind are granted by the retail merchants. I am afraid that the same conditions that obtained when this discount was in force would be created if the attempt were made to put my hon. friend's amendment into operation. As a result of my experience in the case of the retailers' discount I cannot see my way to support the amendment.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I am of the opinion that it is impracticable to put the amendment into execution. If you do not apply the taxation law to returned soldiers I presume you would have to grant a similar exemption to their families, and also to the relatives1 of deceased soldiers. It would be unfair if you did not carry out the exemption to that extent. Imagine, if you will, a customer buying a suit of clothes, or a dress, or a blouse, or some other garment in a large departmental store-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Corsets.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Very well, a pair of corsets. The customer notifies the clerk,. "I am the wife of John Jones, a returned soldier" or she says,, "I. am the daughter of a returned soldier", or "I am from Vancouver and a returned soldier". Just imagine, if you please, the practical impossibility of executing such a proposal. In my judgment under all the circumstances it is not worth considering.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Of course, the hon.
member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) has said that this is an unspeakable and impracticable proposition, and I suppose that is the end of it. However, occasional-

ly we have to differ from the hon. member and decline to follow him slavishly. But the hon. member from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) was for many years a Minister of the Crown, and in experience and service in this House, although not older in years, he is a much older member than my hon. friend from Northumberland,, and with all his experience and ability he has thought it advisable to put this amendment before the committee. I take the responsibility, therefore, of following in the footprints of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve and of saying that this proposal is not only worthy of favourable consideration at the hands of this committee, but that an effort should be made to carry it out. The men who served at the front and won for us the liberty which we now enjoy have earned for themselves for all time to come every possible freedom, and especially freedom from taxation of this kind.
I f at the date of his enlistment any soldier had made it a condition precedent that upon his return home he should be exempt from all war taxation, would not every one in this House and in the country have at once said: "Certainly, you go to the front and do your part, and oh your return you shall never be called upon to pay any war taxes, for we acknowledge that you have done your part and deserve to be exempt from paying any of the expenses of the war''? Would not that have been regarded as an absolutely reasonable proposition? The Minister of Finance states that possibly the returned soldiers do not want to be exempted. Since his Budget Speech was delivered a gathering of returned soldiers in the city of Toronto considered this question and passed a resolution to the following effect:
-whereas the returned soldier and his dependents have already borne their share of the burdens of war, and contributed in invaluable services to the preservation and prosperity of the state, and whereas the recent raise in taxation as set forth in the Budget will increase the difficulty of getting re-established in a productive capacity by greatly augmenting the cost of living, all returned soldiers who have seen overseas service should be exempted from the new taxation for a period of at least five years. That the production of a discharge certificate be considered sufficient evidence of a right to this exemption. That legislation to this effect be enacted by the Parliament of Canada.
That, Sir, is a sufficient answer to the suggestion of the Minister of Finance that our returned men do not want this exemption. We have a right to suppose that this gathering of returned veterans in the city of Toronto-which contributed so much to the success of the war in men and money-expressed the true sentiments of the soldiers generally.
I am not going to labour the question, for it is clear to every one. We say that the soldier has done enough in winning the war, and that we who stayed at home should at least pay his bills while he was away. That is what we are asked to do-to exempt him from contributing towards the payment of our war debt. I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment of my hon. friend.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
merely wish to submit the views of the Quebec Board of Trade and the Ketailers' Association of Quebec as to the collection of these taxes. These views are along the line of ithe argument expressed and set forth hy my hon. friend from Waterloo (Mr. Euler) this afternoon. I have heard many members since the beginning of this debate express the opinion that the best method of collection would be that the tax should be paid by the manufacturer or importer. The hon. the Minister of Finance has not given any answer to these representations and has not presented any argument why this system should not be adopted. The only hon. member who has expressed himself as opposed to that method of collecting the tax is the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), and I must say I have not been much impressed with the soundness of his argument in that regard. I think the proposed mode of collecting the tax will hit the poor consumer more heavily than the wealthy consumer. The poor consumer usually buys from the small trader. The goods generally pass through three or four hands before reaching the small trader. The manufacturer sells to the jobber; the jobber to the wholesale merchant, the wholesale merchant to the retailer, and the tax of one per cent must be collected every time; so that at the end, in many instances, the consumer will have to pay three or four per cent instead of one per cent. On the other hand, the wealthy consumer buys in large stores where the trader usually buys directly from the manufacturer. Moreover, there are many merchants-I know there are some in my own riding-who manufacture many of the articles they sell, and in these cases the tax which will be paid will certainly be less than the tax which has to be paid by those who buy from the country merchant. I wish to read the resolution adopted by the Quebec Board of Trade. It is in the French language but, as the Minister of Finance is a scholar and is versed in both languages, I think it may be read in French, only he will have to listen to me if he wants to know what I read. It is as follows:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
A resolution of the Quebec Board of Trade.
Thursday, May 27, 1920.
Whereas the Government, by their new sales and luxury taxes, are only anxious to lower the cost of living and to restrain extravagance, and at the same time increase their revenue;
The Quebec Board of Trade, after duly considering the new fiscal policy of the Government and without the least intention of protesting against the levying of new taxation, which it deems pressing and unavoidable, has nevertheless made up its mind to respectfully represent to the federal authorities that should they fail to bring in such changes as indicated by the board, they will certainly fail to attain those two laudable objects, and moreover unconsciously countenance fraud to their own detriment:
1. Because, all things considered, the one per cent sales tax hits only the poor consumer who usually buys from the small dealer alone. Now it as known that goods pass through the hands of at least three classes of middlemen before reaching the small dealer; the manufacturer sells to the jobber; the jobber to the wholesale merchant, the wholesale merchant to the retailer, and the tax of one pea* cent must be collected at every stage, so that at the end the poor consumer has to,pay a tax of four per cent upon the goods he buys.
As for the rich consumer the conditions are not the same; he buys generally in the large stores, and the big merchant buys as a rule from the manufacturer directly;
2i Because the collection of these duties will certainly necessitate, in the store as well as in the Finance Department, employment of a large supplementary staff, of clerks and accountants ; and as there is at present a great scarcity of labour, merchants will be forced to draw new hands from the country at a time when production is everywhere so much needed [DOT] this will bring inevitably a new increase in wages and salaries and a consequent increase in the cost of living.
As we already have pointed out the new taxes on sales and on luxuries, under the present circumstances, will certainly tend to stimulate the peddling trade and encourage fraud. It is a well known fact that the small country merchants and the peddlers do not keep books; therefore it will not be an easy task for the officers of the Government to get an accounting of the sales made by these people and to collect the duties: then, they will have to meet with deception on the part of peddlers and country store-ikeepers.
It is a well known fact too that many merchants manufacture, themselves, goods which they retail in their own stores; these merchants will escape the 1 per cent tax on these goods to the great detriment of their less fortunate brethren who have to get the same goods from the wholesale merchants.
Therefore the members of the Quebec Board of Trade respectfully suggest to the Government ito collect directly from the manufacturer or from the importer, at the port of entry, as the case may be, (the taxes on sales and on luxuries. They suggest moreover to the Government to increase from 1 to 2 or 3 per cent the special duty on sales if it has reason to believe that the tax of the 1 per cent collected from the manufacturer alone will not bring sufficient revenue.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
By collecting the tax on sales and on luxuries at the source of supply, or at the port of entry, as the case may be, the said duties will then strike equally every class of buyer, the collection will certainly be more efficient, and trade will not be paralyzed by the impediment and the costly annoyance of a supplementary staff of clerks and accountants.

Now, our experience has been that if you collect it at its source, not only is the tax passed on but a large profit on top of it. Let me illustrate. We put a tax on cigarettes-, following exactly the line of action that is now proposed by hon. gentlemen. That tax was only three cents, but because .it was put on at the source, instead of being collected by the retailer from the purchaser, ten cents additional had to be paid by the purchaser for every package of cigarettes he bought. Instead of increasing the high cost of living we would like, if possible, to reduce that cost; and we know that if the tax is put on at the source, instead of being paid by the purchaser at the time he buys an article, these taxes will tend to inflate rather than to reduce the high cost of living.

speechtext:
We know the tremendous debt which has been created in this country by reason of the war, and that we must of necessity seek fresh channels for getting a revenue to meet the demands icif that debt. W|s also know that some of the Government's taxation proposals have created a tremendous feeling. Nevertheless, in spite of that feeling, the Minister of Finance must do his duty and collect, if possible, the necessary Revenue. Fob. my part I do not entirely concur in his methods of raising revenue. The minister has modified his Budget to sicime extent in regard to the excess taxes on certain lines of business and this no doubt will be appreciated by many merchants, but in taking this action has he not created a prejudice in the minds of merchants engaged in other lines of business, for naturally they will feel that they too should be granted a -similar concession and should pay tax only upon the excess price? I think the minister's action is not popular.
It has been suggested by the retail merchants that as there are only 8,000 -manufacturers and wholesalers in this Dominion the collection of the luxury tax might be confined to them, in preference to spreading
.1460

the collection over some 200,000 retail merchants. By imposing the collection of this tax on the retailer the minister has created a distinct hardship, and any hon. member who has been in the retail business will readily appreciate what I say. The majority of retail merchants are not in a large way of business, and many of the smaller merchants run their stores with very litttle help. But by imposing on them the duty of collecting this sale tax you oblige them to employ extra help to keep track of this collection, and those merchants cannot afford the extra expense. The result will be that thousands of them will he forced out of business and their trade will fall into the hands of the larger merchants, who will, and can, take advantage of the public in many ways that are impossible to the smaller dealer. It is a material advantage to many small consumers to be able to do business with these smaller stores, and I have noticed that in many cases their lower overhead expenses enable the small retailers to dispose of their goods to the public at more favourable' prices to the consumer than the same goods can be bought for from the larger dealers and the departmental stores. It is apparent therefore thait one tendency of collecting this sales tax from the retailer will be a restriction of the retail business to the larger retail stores and the departmental stores. The latter have a decided advantage already over their small competitors, for they are able to buy in large volume and their quick turnover enables them to sell at a very small margin of profit.
I think the minister should give this part of his Budget proposals very serious consideration, and if he will take into his confidence some of these small retail merchants I am sure they will be able to convince him of the necessity of shifting *the collection of this sales tax onto the manufacturers and wholesalers. The latter can very well place the amount of the fax on the price of their goods, so that the retailer will not have to tell his customers that he has no set price, but that it varies according to the amount of war tax any particular line of goods has to bear. As things are, the public will blame the retail merchant, not the Government, simply because they d<o not understand the situation. By making the change. I suggest a great hardship would be removed from these 200,000 retail merchants as well as their customers, and no disadvantage would accrue to the Government, because there can be no doubt that the collection from the manufacturers

and wholesalers will be absolutely effective and will bring in to the treasury the maximum amount of revenue at a much lower cost of collection.
Through the imposition of this sales tax the Government is the most unpopular that Canada has had since Confederation. It is unpopular because of the composition of the Cabinet and because of its doing the wrong thing at the wrong time. It has shown much extravagance at a time "when there should be rigid economy. 'The Budget and the [DOT] method of collecting these new taxes will I am afraid, wreck this Government unless modifications are made in time. The unpopularity of the Minister of Finance and of his colleagues is going to create trouble, and it is just as well that we should talk plainly and warn the Government in time before it gets on the rocks. We know from the large deputations coming to Ottawa that our business men generally are dissatisfied with the excise and sales taxes, and by this time surely the minister ought to be convinced that, some other method should be adopted which will bring into' the treasury a revenue equal to the amount that he hopes to get under this system and at a much less cost.
The biscuit manufacturers have made representations to the members of this House and to the Government against the imposition of a special tax on sugar-coated or powdered biscuits, which will affect only a part of the biscuit industry. It may seem a small matter, but to the biscuit manufacturers it is of great importance, and they say that if the tax is enforced it will throw hundreds of their employees out of work. They have suggested, and I think it is a reasonable suggestion, that instead of confining this tax to a particular line of biscuits it should be applied to all .sweet biscuits, so that there would be no discrimination against certain manufacturers, and at the same time a larger revenue would accrue to the treasury.
Then we have the manufacturers of musical instruments who have made representations to the minister in regard to the manner in which their business will be prejudiced by some of his proposals. Already in Toronto two large musical instrument factories have been closed down. There are hundreds of men out of employment to-day on account of the Government adopting this method of collecting the revenue. The exemption	is up	to $200, but to
limit, it to that will mean the manufacture of a very cheap instrument of much inferior quality and of less

service to the public. If the exemption were increased up to $400 a far superior instrument would be manufactured. It is contended that any piano costing more than $200 is a luxury. I do not consider a piano a luxury, but a necessity, in the homes of the working people. Every member of this House who has visited the homes of working people of this country knows that ninety per cent of them have musical instruments in their homes, either a piano, an organ or some other instrument. I have known many families with three, four and five partly-grown children spending the most entertaining part of their lives in enjoying music in their homes. Take the music away from their homes, and what becomes of these young boys and girls? We all know how music charms and how a musical evening will keep young people home. All of us who have heard the excellent music at a church service or at public gatherings know how soothing it is. How we all praise it! I say that if you take music out of the homes of the working people, these four or five half-grown children without that attraction in the home will go out and spend the evening in the streets and at cheap picture shows and other places that do not tend to the moral welfare of the family so much as having a gathering of the neighbour's children and your own at a musical evening in the home. I trust that the minister will take into consideration the advisability of making some change in this tax. If he goes on as he proposes to do, he will drive the manufacturers out of business, and therefore he will have no opportunity of collecting this revenue. It might result in cheaper instruments being manufactured, but that would be a disadvantage to the people. I trust, therefore, that the minister will raise the exemption to not less than $400, so that he will not drive out of Ontario and the city of Toronto the working men who are engaged in these industries.
The Electrical Supply people have also put forward very strong arguments why they should not be taxed 20 per cent. I do "not know whether the minister has been convinced by their arguments, but I certainly sympathize with these people as well as with other manufacturers. The poor man who has built his home must equip it with electrical fixtures, especially in the large cities where electricity is supplied so cheaply and where it is such a convenience to the householder. This tax will mean that the electrical fixtures for the ordinary home will cost from $30 to $35 extra. Now, that is a very great hardship on a poor man, and he
will have to go back to the old antiquated method of lighting by gas or candle. We should help the working men to progress, not go back. This Government should assist these people to get the modern methods of lighting in their homes, rather than impose this tax upon electrical fixtures.
The fur manufacturers have also put forward very strong arguments. We know how necessary it is in this northern country to have furs for our comfort in winter. Last year we had a severe winter of four or five months. What a hardship this taxing of furs will be to the people of this country who need furs in winter time. This is another matter which should be given serious consideration. It concerns raw materials produced in our own country, and I trust the minister will reconsider the tax he has imposed on these articles.
The Minister of Finance remarked that we must conscript [DOT] the business men of Canada to collect the excise and sales taxes for the Government. It is one thing to conscript them, and another to get results. The Government has had experience of conscription in the past, and I think this latest form of conscription will be just as unpopular. The minister should have got away from that method, but if he must conscript the business men of this country he should have required only the manufacturers and the wholesalers, not the retailers, to collect the tax.
Here is another instance of the tremendous effect these taxes are going to have on industry and the development of our country:
The Canadian Columbia Graphophone Co., Limited, which, in good faith, believing that Canada offered ideal conditions for the manufacture of grafonolas, graphophones and records, bought the plant of the Canadian Aeroplanes, Limited, located in Toronto, on Dufferin and Lappen streets, which occupies 235,000' feet of floor space, for $600,000, paying Canadian people this money.
They are spending $2,000,000 on an equipment ; and were planning to spend $3,000,000 for. materials, when, like a bolt from the blue, came the announcement of the removal of the 7 j per cent special import tax, and the imposition of an excise tax, that, when examined, clearly defined all the instruments and articles produced by the Canadian Columbia Grapho-phone Company as luxuries, thereby handicapping the firm by an excise tax of 20 per cent.
Realize what this means!
This great Canadian undertaking is halted to see what will be done.
Orders have been cancelled for thousands of instruments, and labour is being laid off; and a great Canadian plant, which would soon have been in full blast, giving employment to 4,000 people and a living to 10,000 people, with a pay roll of $120,000 per week, or $6,000,000 per year, held up indefinitely, and Canada, the

There are, let us say, 200,000 retail merchants in this vast country, more than half of whom are very small traders keeping general stores. Probably 50 per cent of them are endowed with keen minds, but are deficient in bookkeeping. I have been in trade for forty yeaTS, and I know something of what the small country store is. There might not be in such a store any article that will be taxable with, perhaps, the exception of ribbons. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Belan-d) mentioned that the sale of a yard of ribbon costing fifteen cents will compel a merchant to make out a monthly report for a cent and a half. That will he a great effort for the merchant, and the Government will secure very little revenue.
There are ways of avoiding this tax. Who is going to collect the tax from the pack-pedlars, the one-horse pedlars, the four-horse pedlars, who are going throughout the country now selling clothes, shoes and other commodities and who do not pay anything for the upkeep of schools, even for the upkeep of the roads on which they travel?

9 p.m. will endeavour to evade this tax. I refer to the favoured few. The wealthy person will go past the retailer down to the wholesaler or manufacturer and will purchase expensive goods there. Let ua see how this tax will affect those
200,000	retailers if they have to make monthly reports. I will ask the minister if this report is supposed to be made at the end or the beginning of every month? The minister gives me no answer. I say, Mr. Chairman, that the collection of the tax in the way the minister proposes will necessitate the employment of an army of clerks in Ottawa and the amount of revenue that will be derived from these retail merchants will not be enough to pay the expenses in connection with the auditing of the accounts. This is going to add thousands of employees to the Civil Service, to say nothing of the enormous scale on which- evasion will be practised. I see that the minister is not paying very much attention to the discussion and I suppose it does not amount to much, so far as he is concerned. Let us consider what a vast number of clerks it will take to audit these two hundred thousand monthly accounts, and we can easily form some idea as to the expense the collection of -this tax will involve. Do you imagine for a moment that fifty per cent of these people will contribute enough to the treasury to pay the clerks who will he engaged in auditing the accounts? The minister's colleague, the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), has built up a business, and he must know that what we need in business more than anything else is to see that our revenue is not eaten up by overhead expenses. Why, -Sir, apart from the large departmental stores in Canada, there are-not a score of merchants in the country who do business of such dimensions. Indeed, many merchants Ido no more than a thousand dollars' worth of business a month, and they handle everything from a needle to an anchor, including grindstones. I can only see a mass of trouble ahead of the minister if he is going to collect the taxes in this way. Every wholesale house throughout the -country has a good accounting system. It keeps a bookkeeper Who has a perfect system of accounting, and it is in every way equipped to keep every sort of record. And the importer has a bonded warehouse and can easily add the taxation to his invoice. In this way you would get -your money in a lump sum, and while it would be considerable its collection would require only one-tenth of the time and clerical work on the part



of the civil servants which would he necessary if the proposed system is followed.
I would suggest to the minister also to lower the valuation of the goods on the manufacturers and importers say 25 per cent more than oil the retailer; and possibly there might be exemptions in regard to goods going to hospitals. I have listened attentively to all that has been said in the discussion of this subject and I have so far failed to hear one argument that really justifies the minister's proposal in regard to the collection of the taxes. The minister says that we need money. We all know that, and1 I do not think that any one has attempted to gainsay the fact. I have not heard any one advancing the argument that there should not be a system of taxation. Matters of detail may have been discussed, but I have not heard any one contend that we do not need to raise money. But the question in dispute is as to the method of collecting that money, and I say that if this proposed system of collection is put into operation it will be the greatest mistake ever perpetrated in this country. I was told that a lady went into a store to buy a $12 hat, but when the merchant said that she had to pay $1.20 upon it she declined to have it; and the same thing applies to shoes and boots.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the minister should realize that it is important to have retail merchants throughout the country, because people will not be induced to go into back settlements unless they know that there are stores in those places where they can obtain their necessities; therefore' nothing should be done to hamper those merchants. When the Act was passed imposing on certain merchants the obligation of affixing stamps by way of duty to the goods they sold, a great deal of trouble resulted and there was a great attempt on the part of many people throughout the country to evade the law. Now this is a monstrous mistake and the minister would de well to consider the representations that have been made to him before putting his proposal into effect. The retail merchant is prepared to bear his share of the burden, but this system will entail a considerable hardship on him. As I have said, it will require a tremendous overhead expenditure to collect this tax. As the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has pointed out, the retailers of the country, under this proposed scheme, would virtually be in the employ of the Government, doing work for which they would not be paid, and you could not blame them for being antagonistic to such a proposal. If the minister is anxious to put

money into the treasury, let him impose a tax on the manufacturer and the importer, and that will cover all. But this is a most stupendous and stupid piece of business, for the reason that the overhead1 expenses in-the collection of the tax will consume all the revenue derived.

speechtext:
If the minister has
definitely made up his mind to adhere to this method of collecting, I do not suppose that it is of much use to discuss the matter further. But if as he said this afternoon -and I commend him for the expression- he is still keeping an open mind to learn whatever can be learned, I respectfully say that I hope that even yet he will reconsider this matter. It seems to me that the arguments that have been advanced in favour of the present system are not strong, while the arguments in support of a different system appear to me to be almost unanswerable. There is one reason my 'hon. friend might advance for his present system; I wonder if it has been in the back of his head all the time and he has been too bashful to express it. If he collects this tax at the source, the source being either the manufacturer, the wholesaler or possibly the importer,-at all events the wholesaler,-he will not get the tax once but under the system that he is adopting he is going to get the tax at least three or four times. He can multiply this tax to the consumer. For my hon. friend to argue that by this system he is going to prevent an increase in the cost of living is quite beyond my comprehension. I think it is entirely a mistake on his part. Let us take an illustration. Suppose a large manufacturer is about to sell $400 or $500 worth of high class goods to a wholesaler. Of course, the tax is not imposed on the whole value of the goods. The tax is only on the excess and' it is only the excess that we are now taking into account. That excess will be, say, $100-it is possible that on goods of a value of $400 or $500 there will be $100 of excess. On that excess there will be a tax of $15 when the wholesaler buys the goods. There is a tax on the profits piling up all the time but we need not stop to consider that because that is something that is created by the tax. The wholesaler pays $115 for the taxable portion of the goods. Adding to that his profit before he sells to anybody else he will sell at an advance, I will say, at the moderate rate of ten per cent. That ten per cent enters into the selling price and it is on the selling price that you are levying the tax. The wholesaler will sell those goods at $115 plus

a profit, and the tax, when the goods get into the hands of the retailer, will toe at least $17.25. Thus the goods pass to the retailer. The retailer also gets his profit, and he fixes his selling price after he has added his profit. You will find that in that transaction on goods passing only through three hands-it may be through four by including the jobber-under your system, you will collect at least three taxes. But, instead of getting 15 per cent as my hon. friend proposes, the tax on these goods, passing through the hands of these three different parties, will amount to about 60 per cent, and if you put the jobber in between the manufacturer and the wholesaler, instead of that parcel of goods paying 15 per cent, it pays nearly 100 per cent into the treasury. If my hon.	friend w'ants
to get the money in that	way, I
admit at once that he	is going to
get it by collecting three or four taxes instead of one. And it all comes down in the end to the consumer. Does any one imagine for a moment that the manufacturer, the wholesaler or the retailer is going to pay that tax without adding it to his price? What was urged by so many hon. members here to-day, what was urged by the French Chamber of Commerce of Montreal in the resolution that I presented last night, what was urged by the Quebec Board of Trade in the' resolution read to-day by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), what was urged by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr.' Euler) and by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin) are all arguments why the tax should be levied at' the source. I admit that if my hon. friend adopts that plan he will only get the tax once, but if he says frankly that he wants to get it three or four times I can understand what he is driving at. If that is his idea, do not ask the people to believe that they are only paying 15 per cent when they are paying 60 or 70 per cent and possibly even more. I believe that is a mistake. If my hon. friend says that he has ito have it, that is an argument that is understandable.
My hon. friend from Standstead . (Mr. Baldwin) has not exaggerated the case when he speaks of the irritation, worry and unnecessary expenditure that will be caused to retailers by the system which my hon. friend proposes. I do not want to dwell on the situation longer. It seems to me that there is everything to be said in favour of direct taxation at the source unless my hon. friend says that he cannot 220*
get enough at the source and "hat he must get it over and over again in order to get his revenue. But he has not put it on that ground and I do respectfully ask him before this Bill is finally through to give consideration to the views'which have been so strongly expressed to-night by hon. members of this House.
