Mr. J. (E. FONTAINE (Hull) (Translation) : Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of detaining the House very long; yet, taxation being levied upon necessaries of life, taxation- which caused such tan upheaval throughout this country and was the occasion for such loud protests, I -feel it to be my duty -to offer some observations on behalf of the constituents I have the privilege of representing.
There is in the city of Hull a retailers' association, a most important organization of which our foremost merchants are members, which last night, at a special meeting, passed a resolution in condemnation of the method advocated by the Government for the levying of taxation. I was confident that, -having altered the system of taxation as to -some commodities, the hon. Minister of Finance would agree to change the method df gathering those taxes.
The retail merchants lare rightfully complaining about the trouble and expenses it is going to entail to them. To my mind, it would be fairer -to have those taxes collected at the fountain head, from the manufacturer. A few moments ago, T heard the hon. Minister of Finance state that certain commodities would be taxed at the very fount olf production because they are not necessaries of life, for instance, pianos, phonographs, and so forth. Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that such articles as cut glass, velvet, silk, laces, are not essentials, and yet the hon. Minister of Finance will cause the retail merchant to collect the tax upon them. His reason for so doing is by no means conclusive, since in- the case of patent medicines which, far from being luxuries, are absolutely necessary, he has the tax oollected from the manufacturing establishment itself.

I think that the Government .ought to grant the request of all the retailers of this country. After all, Mr. Chairman, it cannot 'be out of stubbornness that this association aisk that the burden of collecting these taxes should not rest upon them. As it was said by many hon. members who spoke before me, it might favour fraud" and force the consumer to pay higher prices for, say what you may, it will always be an easy thing to humbug him.
Once again I wish to act tas the spokesman of the Association of Retail Merchants of Hull who have requested me to place their case before the House; I do so with pleasure and I ask the -hon. minister, in their name and in the name of all the citizens of this country, to give -heed to their representations and to find a way for collecting these taxes which will not be -such a heavy burden on the retailer. If the tax were collected from the manufacturer 15 or 20 per cent would be added to the price of the goods and the tax thus paid by the wholesaler iat the time of his purchase; he in turn would include the tax in the price of the goods when selling them to the retailer. Of course, in the long run, the consumer would pay the duty, but he would not notice it, and besides the retail merchant would be relieved of all this load of responsibility.
Mr. Chairman, I humbly submit that the hon. minister should accede to the requests of the many hon. members, who are only voicing the sentiments of the country when they aek that a different system be devised for the collection of this tax. We are not criticising the tax itself at the present time; we understand that it must be imposed, that it is absolutely necessary as things stand to-day; however, it is unfortunate that the Government should have led the country into this position-I understand that -this question cannot be discussed in committee. Besides I mentioned this in my speech on the Budget, when I reproached the Government with having put us in a position where the imposition of these taxes is a matter of necessity. I-f there had been more economy, less extravagance, less scandal, we would not find o/urselves in this position to-day; however, since the thing is done, II think the Government should at least do its utmost not to make things so hard for certain classes of the community and not to overburden the retail merchants whose time must be given entirely to their business and who should not be forced by the Gov-

eminent to act in the capacity of tax collectors.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
It appears to me that the minister is quite oorreot in his description of the collection of the tax, that is, through the method he proposes it is obviously to be collected only once, and that from the retailer. There can 'be no doubt of that because the words "sold separately" occur in the first clause, and the second clause makes that even more distinct. So I think my hon. friend from Shelburne and' Queen's (Mr. Fielding)-with whom I agree on some other points-is not correct in saying that the tax would be passed on three or four times before the final sale.
I suggest to the minister, however, that I am still very strongly of opinion that it is highly desirable for him to change the mode of collection. I stated that the other day, and when the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) challenged me on the point of my proposed change raising the cost of the commodity to the consumer, I said undoubtedly it would, because if the tax is collected at the fountain head it would have to be passed on, and it would be passed on on each invoice. But instead of being, collected from 200,000 people, as is proposed here, the tax would be collected from 7,000 ot 8,000 people. The accounting system of these 7,000 or
8,000	would obviously be accurate, and the department could walk in there and be sure they were getting all that was coming to them, because all these people are almost obliged under the laws of the country to keep an accurate account of every sale, and everything has to be audited by competent men. But these conditions do not obtain with the retailer. As my hon. friend has pointed out, there are tens of thousands of merchants in this country who are not doing $1,000 worth of business- a day, or even a week/ and many of them not even- in a month, and it is unfair and unreasonable in my judgment for the Government to impress 200,000 men into the service of the country to collect taxes for which work they receive no remuneration whatever. They will be put to a very great expense. My hon. friend from North Oxford said $5 would cover it. If he had said $500 he would have been short of the mark, and so far as the large establishments are concerned it will be nearer $5,000. I say it is scarcely right to impress these men all over the country, and some women-for there are women shopkeepers-into the Government service without any remuneration. Further, it puts every one of these vendors into the position of possibly offending their customers, and that is a very undesirable thing. If there is one thing above another that a merchant tries to avoid, it is to offend anybody who is trading with him. He would do almost anything rather than that, because an offended customer means a loss of trade. It is a very unpopular thing to be a tax-collector; that is admitted by all. It is bad enough to pay taxes, but I believe it is worse to collect them. From the abuse I have heard some tax-collectors get around different parts of the country, I am sure their position is no sinecure. The minister has made it clear to my mind that there are some valid reasons why this tax should only be collected once, and if it could be done by the wholesaler I think that is the most desirable way. I admit that if the tax' is collected at the fountain head it will be passed on and the result will be that the customer will pay more than the Government will receive. There is no doubt about that. It is very much like a man buying a barrel of spirits and instead of paying -a duty of $2 a gallon on the forty gallons, collecting the tax over the bar on every glass sold out of that barrel. That is practically the principle the minister proposes to follow. We are going to have 200,000 tax-collectors. The retail merchants, who have gone on record in this respect, have stated that they do not think they should -be impressed into the Government service in this way. They say they are willing to do all that is reasonable, but I submit to the, minister that it is not in accordance with British fair play to impress 200,000 people, who have their living to earn-I was -a merchant for a good many years and I know that they do not get their money any too readily-into the Government Service in this way without any remuneration. These retail merchants lose a great deal that is on their books and some of these luxury taxes will be lost on the books of these firms as soon as they are put on. The Government will also want a statement from every -retailer. Now that cannot be prepared readily. -Some merchants are not expert accountants. In the old days many of them did not keep books so far as cash was concerned. If they had money in the bank and in their pockets they did not worry. The larger establishments, making up about ten or fifteen per cent of -all the stores in the country, have very good accounting systems. That remark, however, does not apply to the average retailer. Therefore, w-e cannot expect them to comply with the requirements of the depart-

ment very readily and without a great deal of trouble and considerable expense. Though by this method I am suggesting the taxpayer would pay a little more, he would pay it without knowing it, but under the njethod proposed by the minister he is going to be confronted with the tax every time he buys. The minister says that that is what he wants. Well, he will certainly bring it home to the buyer, but it will not be very palatable to him. There is many a man who takes a dose without knowing what is in it, and what the results will be, who would have be-sitated to take it if he had known the consequences. It is the same with this tax. -It is going to be unpalatable in its present form, and it is going to be difficult to collect. It is going to put on those who pay the tax into the treasury the obligation of collecting taxes from their clients, whom they want to be their best friends. The minister has expressed himself as having an open mind on this question, and I believe: he has. That benign smile of his shows that he has a very warm spot in his heart for the argument we are putting up. I do not want to use any undue pressure, or to make any threats, or do anything of that sort, but I do appeal to the minister in the interests of the people as a whole, and of the merchants in particular, and their Customers too, to reconsider the method of collecting the tax. I believe my hon. friend from. Red Deer will admit that if a man is paying a tax that he does not know he is paying, it is not half so unpalatable.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I am sure the House must be delighted with the minister for bringing 
on this discussion, if for no other reason than to hear the confession of the hon. member for Brantford of his conversion from his protectionist ideas. He has declared himself without doubt and beyond question to-night, and I sincerely trust that he will not have reason to change his attitude on some other occasion. I remember an occasion not long since when he appealed to the former Minister of Finance to "have a heart." To-night he almost looked as if he was asking the present Minister of Finance to "have a heart," though in another direction altogether. I shall not attempt to give the reasons for this.
In the Budget speech the Minister of Finance defined very clearly his attitude in regard to these taxes. In this printed copy of the Budget speech, in the part which the editor has headed "Luxury Taxes" I find this opening sentence,, which is very convincing to me at least:
Not only is more revenue necessary but extravagant and luxurious expenditure ought to be checked. Just so long as expenditure on nonessentials and extravagant expenditure continues, just so much longer will the drop in the value of essentials be postponed. On those having income more than necessary for properly maintaining themselves and families, there rests a special duty of saving whenever possible and in this manner adding to the available financial resources for development and for industrial undertakings. Extravagant buying should stop.
Since these Budget proposals have been brought doum the minister has stated many times in the House and elsewhere that he is prepared to stand or fall by them as introduced. That is the principle of collecting from the retailer on certain specific articles and from the wholesaler on others.
I may say at the outset that I am sorry the minister has taken that stand, because I ivould have preferred a different method of collecting the tax. Just the same, it is my desire that the minister shall get down to business as soon as possible, and it is not my intention to delay the committee very long on the present occasion. I may assure the committee at once that it is my intention to give the minister all assistance necessary in order to put this schedule into workable operation. I want, however, to go on record at the same time as to the method I would suggest if I had the say or if I had been consulted in the matter before it reached this stage.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has taken exception to this method, as have also many other speakers who have preceded me in this dis-

cussion. Some of them have claimed that one method would be preferable and some, another, for reasons assigned. I am sorry I cannot see eye to eye with my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) in the method he suggests, and the same method has been suggested by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt). The argument will not stand analysis to any great extent. The proposition made by my hon. friend is that the tax shall be collected at the source of supply. Let us see what that means, taking the simple tax of one per cent on sales. I take for my illustration a raw material, say wool. The wool broker imports a quantity of wool, on which quantity he pays to the Government a tax of one per cent, and 'I will take the figure of one dollar. The broker passes that on to the manufacturer, and, of course the broker will charge a reasonable profit on that one per cent tax; he will add it to the price of the material. That means that the manufacturer will pay the broker $1.25 for that one dollar's worth of tax. The manufacturer, of course, will add on one per cent he has to pay to the Government plus his profit. That means $1 on to the $1.25, or $2.25, plus the manufacturer's reasonable profit which will be 56 cents, making a total cost from the manufacturer to the wholesaler of $2.81. The wholesaler adds on his one per cent which goes to the Government, plus his profit, which, on a moderate estimate will be at least 25 per cent, and sometimes it is more 4han that. The wholesaler finds that he has an item of $3.81 to account for, to which he adds his 25 per cent profit, or 95 cents, making a total of $4.76, the cost to the retailer. The retailer in turn will pass that on to his customer with his profit added. I can speak from experience and I know with certainty that the retailer who adds a mere bagatelle of 25 per cent to the cost of his 'commodity-in the case I have assumed that would represent $1.44-will find that an item of one dollar which the broker paid to the Government in the initial stage has risen, through the process of transmission from one stage to another, to the total sum of $6.20 when it reaches the consumer. This, in a nutshell, means that the Government will receive the sum of $3 which amounts to $6.20 by the time it reaches the consumer. In other words, out of $6.20 paid by the consumer for the tax item on the merchandise purchased, the Government will receive only the sum of $3. That is a good argument against collecting the tax back at the source of supply, because if you collect the other tax as well as that at the
source of supply, it will also multiply in geometrical proportion as it goes from one stage to another. I am not, therefore, in favour of this systehi of collection. I know that this system has been endorsed 'by the Retail Merchants Association,
10 p.m. but they are only a body of men who perhaps have not considered this matter as fully as they might have done. A few weeks ago they were in favour of another system, and perhaps tomorrow they will be in favour of a different system from the one selected to-day.
I might say at once that I am in favour of a "tax on turnover" or "a tax on sales," and that would undoubtedly be the ideal system. It would be simple in operation and inexpensive to collect, and it would give the Government the maximum of returns for the minimum cost. Further, the maximum of collections would be received by the Government at the least cost to the consumer.
The proposition as it is before the committee at the present time embodies several systems of collection. The principal method of collection which has engaged so much attention since the Budget was announced was the excise tax collected by the retailer from the consumer; but we have, too, a tax on the total amount of the specific item, also a tax on the amount in excess of a specific amount, and a tax on the total amount of certain specific .articles, as well .as a tax collected by the retailer from the consumer, and a tax collected from the importer or manufacturer on certain other items on the list as the case may be. We have all these systems embodied in this amended resolution; but, notwithstanding all this, the minister has deter-, mined that he is bound to stand or fall by the system; that conclusion he has enunciated before the committee. There is no use wasting any further time with this discussion; but nevertheless, I wish to show further the reasons why I prefer the "sales tax" or tax on "turn-over" to the tax on so-called luxuries and so forth, when collected either from the importer, manufacturer, or retailer.
The United States have had a luxury tax in force during the past year from the first of May last, and their experience should be some guidance to us. I may say that the system adopted by them is somewhat different from that adopted by the Minister of Finance. Their system applies entirely on the amount in excess of a specific amount named in their schedule and their list of items is not nearly as large as the

speechtext: Would it do for this Government to have so much money to spend?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Well, it would be a good thing for the country to have that much money. Now, Mr. Chairman, in looking

over the Budget Speech of the Minister of Finance, I find at page 16 of the report as printed by the department that the revenue anticipated during the current year is $381,000,000 odd; the expenditure is $549,000,000 odd, and the deficit $168,000,000. These are the figures, roughly. They may not be absolutely correct, but that is my reading of them and if I am wrong I trust the minister will correct me. Now that seems to me to present a huge problem for the Government and the country to face, and if we could adopt a system such as is described in the article I have read I could see daylight through the difficulties that are now facing us. I shall not detain the committee much longer, but I desire to refer to one or two of the main objections that have been advanced by some hon. gentlemen. The Minister of Finance has been kind enough to admit that the explanation which I gave to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) was correct; that is to say, that where a manufacturer sells direct to a consumer then the tax of one per cent and the excise tax, or whatever else you choose to call it, is paid at the same time. There is another proposition that might be considered in that connection, and I gather from what the Minister of Finance has said that he either has dealt with it or intends to do so. I refer to the case where a manufacturer sells direct to the retailer. In cases of that kind, the retailer who is in a position to buy direct from the manufacturer or import direct from the original sources in the manufacturing centres of the Old Land will be at an advantage of two per cent over the smaller retailers throughout the country. That feature should be considered and attended to. There are a few items in the schedule to which I would call the attention of the minister, and I shall run over them briefly so that the committee may know what they are. I find in the list originally prepared-whether it is correct "or not I am not sure- that the Minister of Finance has placed a tax on ham and bacon while he is placing sausages on the free list. So far as this article of food is concerned, I must say that I differ from Mark Twain. Mark Twain said he liked sausages because he knew what he was eating, and for the same reason I do not like them. I should like to know why the department decided to make sausages free, while taxing ham and bacon. Then I find that baby foods and breakfast foods are taxable, while food for cattle and hogs is free. That seems remarkable. Then there is an amendment in regard to ribbons. Ribbons
are changed and an exemption is provided in that case. He exempts typewriting ribbons.
Mr. McMAjSTER: Will that apply to the ribbons worn by stenographers?

I think I am safe in saying that there is not a household in Canada that does not receive a catalogue at least from one of the great houses, and many receive them from several houses. Yet this Royal Commission reported they have been losing between seventydive and eighty million pounds annually that they have not yet been able to find -any means of collecting. Now, let me give you a homely illustration with regard to that. Go into the smallest city that you can find in the Dominion of Canada and ask the tax collector if he finds it very easy to collect the income tax equitably from all the people who pay it simply for the maintenance of the public school in that village, and see what answer you will get. He will tell you at once that the most difficult thing to be equitably collected is the income tax, and the only way you are going to do it equitably at all is to have an absolute head tax which everybody shall pay. That is what the collector will tell you. However I do not wish do dwell upon that. I. believe the plan of collecting the luxury tax through the excise method is a good one. I believe if put into proper operation it will yield 4 large revenue and will have the very result that the minister hopes for.
But just a word about the details. The last time I spoke on this subject I gave the House some figures I had worked out in connection with a certain retail store, which figures I claim are not over the average. I found there were 100 transactions in one day's business, and that it would take 43

pages of foolscap to contain the monthly statement to be transmitted to the department. On the same average that that retailer was collecting on his sales-and he sells about the usual kind of goods retailed throughout this country-in order to collect $1,000,000 in taxes 10,000,000 entries would be necessary on the statements transmitted to the department. Every Single one of those statements will have to 'be checked against the accompanying slips if the department is to be -certain of the correctness of the returns. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that there must be some misunderstanding as to the number of retail storekeepers in this country, for if there are 200,000 or 250,000, that is equivalent to one storekeeper to every 45 or 30 people, which does seem unreasonable. Basing my estimate on districts I am familiar with, I would say that there is about one store to every 250 or
400 people. But even that means that we have to go back to something like 40,000 storekeepers to collect this tax. We all know that tax collection is not tod easy, and that the fewer people you have to deal with the more productive the tax will be, the more economically it will be collected; and as some one has said, you will " get your feathers with the least squawking possible." The very fact that this tax has caused so much commotion is a warning to the minister to get it, if possible, at the point of production as the member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), has suggested. I fully agree with him that that is the point at which this tax should be applied. It seems to me that the minister said he believed that would be the most economical for the Government, and probably the most productive. Then what are the objections to that method? Following his mind as nearly as I can, I judge that it is because the tax, not being taken directly out of the consumer's pocket, becomes an indirect tax. That will apply mainly to the luxury tax. I have understood that the department is not calculating that a very great sum is going to be derived from this tax, perhaps $10,000,000 or $15,000,000, but that the bulk of the amount that will be raised by these new taxes will be raised by the one per cent tax. I very much fear that the luxury tax will practically put out of business many firms. In trying to get some ideas on this tax I ran across the fact the other day that in Spain they had a tax on sales of .14 per cent. It was afterwards reduced to 10 per cent and later to 6 per cent. Both Spanish and English economists agree that that tax was the cause of the ruin of Spanish industry and Spanish agriculture. Now this tax on luxuries is going to exceed on the average this 14'per cent tax in Spain. I agree that taxes should be collected where there is ability to pay, but at the same time you must have regard to the existence of businesses, and some businesses are sure to be greatly hampered and very likely ruined by the excessive amount of these taxes. Hence, I judge they will exist for only a very short time. After they have been applied for a year I believe they will be ameliorated, if not entirely wiped out.
Now the department has had some experience in the collection of a tax of this kind-experience in two ways. I have understood from members of the department that the tax on matches, amounting to over $1,500,000, is being collected by about three

men. On the other hand, the stamp taxes have caused untold anxiety to the department, very much expense and a great deal of perturbation. There have been prosecutions all over the country for violations of the Act respecting this tax which is collected from the consumer. It seems to me that this should be a warning to the Government as to what is likely to happen when this luxury tax is applied, if it is placed on the consumer instead oif at the point of production.
There are other things I might say but I think those are the most important.

There is a little information I should like to get from the Minister of Finance. I should like to know if he or his department has made any estimate as to how much it is going to cost the country to collect this tax from the retailer; how many officials .will be employed at headquarters at Ottawa to check the returns as they come in; and how many will be employed all over the country to see that the retailers make out the returns properly and -record the sale of every article which should pay a tax. It seems to me that it will take an army of officials, anywhere from 5,000 to 10,000, to look after the collection of this tax. That means not only a great initial expense to the country, but I presume that when we get through with our present financial difficulties this tax will be dropped, and that these 5,000 or 10,000 officials which the minister proposes to take from the farm, the fisheries, the mines, and lumbering camps, will be added to the already overmanned Civil Service. If there is any possible way of collecting this tax without appointing more officials, it should certainly be done. I think I understood the minister to say this afternoon that -practically no Officials had yet been added to the department. My information from a reliable source is that the very first day after the minister made his Budget Speech fifty new officials were taken on by the Inland Revenue Department to make out the proper forms in connection with this tax. It seems to me that to take men out of productive industry and put them into a position where they are not producers, but drones, especially in view of the country's finances, is to do the very opposite of what we should do. We should be getting men out df non-productive employment into work where they would be real producers. I would strongly urge on the minister that

the proper place to apply this tax is at the source of the goods.
The minister said in answer to a question that this resolution should be considered separately from the one dealing with the one per cent tax. But the three taxes dovetail so -into one another that we cannot discuss them separately: the one per cent tax must first be got from the manufacturer selling to the wholesaler, secondly, from the wholesaler selling to the retailer, and thirdly comes this luxury tax which is collected by the retailer. I repeat that the proper place to apply this tax is at the source of supply, where the article is imported or manufactured, instead of having an army of officials added to the present staff to look after the collection of the tax. Then the Government wmuld not have' to have these officials going round seeing that the retailer made up a proper statement. By this method they wmuld get every dollar of taxation that was due, and would get far more revenue than they will under this method proposed by the Minister of Finance.

He made his speech in this 'House and we were all very much pleased, I have no doubt, to hear the hon. gentleman; and for two weeks the eloquence of hon. members resounded through the Chamber telling of the great courage which the Minister of Finance had displayed in the manner in which he had brought, down his Budget asking the people to- dance to the tune that he at that time was playing. He had thousands of copies of that speech prepared -for distribution. I did not ask the minister why that speech was printed, but I take it for granted that the object was to permit hon; members to send it broadcast over the country in order to instruct the merchants, retailers and wholesalers, and all those engaged in business transactions from the Atlantic to the Pacific, as to what would be expected of them. That speech has been distributed; it is in the -hands of all business people. For ten days they have "carried on", and I have no doubt -the statement that has been made is correct, that a very large number of merchants have been collecting the tax. Whether it was proper or improper was not a question for them; they had to obey the law. They have collected this money, and notwithstanding that my hon. friend from East Lambton says that the peo-ple in his town were well satisfied, the minister co-mes- and says: "I am going to change all that. We were all wrong. The retail dealers, the business men who sent telegrams and circular letters, the boards of trade who sent petitions are all right and I am all wrong, and therefore I am going to change this thing". I would ask my hon. friend if he is going to stand by the Budget he has brought down or whether we are to expect that in a day or two, after he has received some letters and telegrams from

wholesaler, or the importer-as it is my opinion they should be-that will mean added .cost to the consumer because that expense will ultimately reach the consumer. I am not so sure that he is right in that regard. The first thing that a merchant, in the country or in the city, will have to do will be to make additions to his staff to look after the extra clerical work necessarily involved in the collection of these taxes.
A few days ago I had representations from a merchant in my constituency-out o.f many I have had-who has three retail stores. He tells me that not only will the added expense to his business be very great, but that he practically will have to scrap his . whole sales system and introduce a new plan in order to 'furnish the Finance Department with the extra invoices they require. The whole of that expense will he added to the cost of the business done by the merchant and it will simply mean an addition to the price to the consumer. I am therefore not so sure that the method of collecting from the manufacturer, the wholesaler or the importer will prove more expensive in operation than the method proposed by the Minister of Finance. And even if that result did follow, the economy that could be secured in the administration of these taxes at Ottawa-and elsewhere throughout Canada where offices would1 have to be established by the .minister-would justify the method of collecting these taxes from the importer, the manufacturer and the wholesaler. It is essential, Mr. Chairman, that these taxes be paid if we are going at the business seriously. There is nothing that will prove more demoralizing -to the people of this country than for the impression to grow in the public mind that these taxes can be evaded; and I am very certain of this-that the minister cannot devise machinery that will adequately insure their collection by all the retailers. That, to my mind, forms one of the strongest justifications for a change in method.
I would therefore urge, in the best of good temper, that my hon. friend should reconsider the matter, and that he accept the suggestions that have come-not only from hon. gentlemen on this side but even with greater .force from members on his own side. We all want to arrive at the best solution of this question; I am sure of that. I for one appreciate the difficulties that confront the Finance Minister-but after all I am convinced that this method of collecting taxes from the retailers will not only be unpopular throughout the country-which per-

haps does not matter so much-but will prove expensive, and inadequate, and will lead to wholesale violation of the law. That is not to be desired in any system of collecting taxes. We have discussed the matter now, Mr. Chairman, for a couple of hours, and perhaps, my remarks might more properly come under section 2, but I understand that I shall be in order in moving an amendment. I therefore move:
That the resolution be amended by striking therefrom the second paragraph of the said resolution and substituting therefor the following paragraph:
"That the excise taxes as imposed by the preceding resolution shall be paid by the manufacturer, or wholesaler at the time of sale, or on importations at the time of importation in addition to the duties of customs already imposed ; and by the manufacturer or wholesaler, to His Majesty in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed."

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I wish to say a word or two regarding the amendment just submitted, and to give some further reasons why I think the proposal of the minister is the better plan. First of all we must not forget that we have a vast sum to raise annually, and this money must be obtained through the customs and by direct taxation. The proposal to collect luxury taxes through the retail merchants is, I admit, surrounded with difficulty; but no great reform or change in the mode of collecting taxes could ever be undertaken without difficulty. The minister has told us how these difficulties will be overcome, but he has not all his plans formulated.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: That is a good word.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: However, he tells us what taxes will be collected, that they will be collected from those who -are best able to pay them, and the method of collecting them. Now I want, if I can, to point out the advantages that are involved to the people of Canada, and when I speak of the people of Canada .1 speak of them as represented by the Government. The Government of Canada represent the people of this country.	'

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Oh, no.
Mr. LOGGIE-: Well, this Parliament represents the people.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Not this Government at any rate.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I want, if I can, to point out some advantages that accrue to the

people of Canada in connection with raising the necessary revenue. The tax on luxuries, collected through the retail merchants as proposed, will on the original value of imports give the Government about 875 per cent more revenue, without any extra cost to the consumer. If it does that, is it not a fair guess that it will save the consumer taxes from some other source? But it does more than that. It impresses buyers of luxuries with the fact that they are directly paying some of our war expenditures, and it fosters the buying of goods that are not classed as luxuries. The proposal is definite and clear that goods coming under the class of luxuries are passed on to the consuming public on the basis of the retailer putting his profit only on the cost of the goods under the regular tariff. Then the retailer says to the consumer: In order to pay interest on the war debt the Government requires an extra ten per cent on any high class article that is designated a luxury. And the whole of that tax goes into the coffers of the people of Canada, represented by the Government.
Now, in order to illustrate to hon. gentlemen opposite in the clearest manner possible *what I have been stating, I have 'here two tables illustrating the results. I take an invoice of silks and laces valued at the custom house at $10,000:
Luxury tax paid by importer and absorbed in
sales:-
Invoice of silks and laces	 $10,000
Add luxury tax if by customs tax....	1,000
Cost of goods to wholesaler	 $11,000
Add wholesaler's profits, 25 per cent.. 2,750
Cost of goods to retailer	 $13,750
Add retailer's profit	 6,875
Cost of goods to consumers	 $20,625

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman
permit me a question? Is that fifty per cent retailer's profit real or fictitious?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: That is the average profit of a retailer selling silks. I do not think he could afford to sell silks at less than fifty per cent profit.	.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: That is a pretty good profit.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Now, the point I want to make is that on those goods which cost the consumer $20,625 the Government gets only $1,000 if the tax is collected on the principle of the amendment before the House. But let me now point out what tax will accrue to the treasury if the Government's proposal is adopted:
Luxury tax collected by the retailer:-
Invoice of silks and laces	 $10,000
Add wholesaler's profit, 25 per cent.. 2,500
Cost of goods to retailer	 $12,500
Add retailer's profit, 50 per cent		6,250

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Add 10 per cent luxury tax	 1,875
Cost of goods to consumers	 $20,625
In-this case the cost to the consumer is $20,625, or exactly the same as if the tax were collected through the customs house and the Government got only $1,000, whereas in this case they get $1,875, or 875 per cent more. That is positively correct as far as I can figure it, and if hon. gentlemen opposite can point out any error I shall be glad to hear from them.
I have another table which is practically the same in principle, but I put the profits at a different rate, that is to- say, I have made the wholesaler's profit 10 per cent and the retailer's profit 25 per cent. Here the amount paid to the Government through the customs would be $1,000, but if paid through the retailer would be $1,375. Ile-member, Mr. Chairman, the cost to the consumer is the same, but these profits are not as they Teally would be, that is to say, they are much less than what the consumer would pay. However, the point I want to make is that allowing a profit of 25 per cent to the -wholesaler and 50 per cent to the retailer the Government would get 875 per cent more money, and the consumer would not pay a dollar more, under the proposals of the Minister of Finance. So far as I am concerned, therefore, I am prepared to vote against the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one or two things ought to be pointed out before the vote on the amendment is proceeded with. Rightly or wrongly, a good many things have been said on the question of checking extravagance and waste, and I wonder if we are at all sincere in what we say. 1 wonder if we realize that what is proposed is that the poor man's boots shall be taxed with the cost of the rich man's luxuries. That is what this amendment amounts to. What is proposed is that instead of this tax being paid by the man who can afford to pay it when he makes the expenditure, it should be levied on the manufacturer or wholesaler as the case may be. Is anyone green enough to imagine for one minute that the goods on the shelves of the wholesaler or in the warehouse and factories of the manufacturer are going to be taxed from time to time in connection with this

luxury tax? Under the amendment the luxury tax will become part of the general cost of that manufacture, and you ask us to say that the poor man shall make up that cost. In a boot factory you have workmen's rough boots at say $4 or $5 or $6 a pair, and also boots costing $18 and $20 a pair. The whole effect of the amendment is to say that to that cost of the workmen's boot shall be added the costs to which the manufacturer is put because he carries on the manufacture of more highly priced lines. The taxes would not be luxury taxes at all in that case. They would be taxes on expenditure. They would be added costs to the manufacturer, which he could place just where he pleased, and if he found it easier to charge the whole of it on his cheaper lines of goods, leaving it off the more expensive he could do so. I do not believe that the hon. gentleman intends any such result, but that can only be the result. There is another thing, which I am absolutely sure was not intended at all, which goes to show how easy it is to make errors of this kind. The amendment seeks to replace section 2 with the following:
That the excise taxes as imposed by the preceding resolution shall be paid by the manufacturer or wholesaler at the time of sale, or on importations at the time of importation in addition to the duties of customs already imposed ;
Now, mark it, mark it.-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Mark it well.
There are only two interests that are called upon to pay that tax, the manufacturer or the wholesaler. The retailer can import as much as he likes without paying any tax, because the word "importer" does not appear in the amendment, but simply the manufacturer or wholesaler.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: What about the individual?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
And there is nothing in the amendment to prevent the individual bringing in the highest-priced motors and automobiles without paying taxes. I am sure that the hon. gentleman could hardly have intended such a result as that. I am sure that the insinuation^ which could be easily made, that this is a studied worked-out policy in the interests of some retail concern would be false. It might be insinuated that this is something which has been worked up to enable some particular backers of my hon. friend to get in their automobiles free or that is something under which the grain growers, selling as they do direct to the public, and therefore being

neitiher manufacturers nor wholesalers, could entirely escape the tax; but I do not believe for one minute that any of those considerations was present with my hon. friend. I simply desire to point out to him just what his amendment means-just what its effect would be. For what reason? The reason is manifest.
I have been charged with changing my mind. I have changed my mind. I change my mind when it is shown to me that I am wrong, but I do not change my mind upon pressure or influence. Hon. gentlemen talk about the number of retailers in this country. Several speakers have mentioned 200,000. My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) got it up to between 400,000 and 500,000, while my hon. friend (Mr. Orerar) got it down to a much closer figure. If there are 200,000 retailers, there are 200,000 reasons for changing one's mind if pressure or influence is to be a reason why one should change one's mind. If any hon. gentleman can show that this amendment will help the common people of this country, and by that I mean all those iwho buy goods, and who are not manufacturers, not wholesalers, not retailers, and will not add to their costs, I will change my mind. But I am not changing my mind because 50,000 or 200,000 retail merchants want me to change it. I appeal to my hon. friend to forget for one moment that he and I do not agree. I would ask him to try to remember some of the principles for which he says he can honestly stand. I would ask him to remember what he thinks about a tax that can be made the source of an added profit to a manufacturer as against a suffering consuming public. My words are not quite the same as his; but the idea is exactly the same. And to-day he is faced with an opportunity of placing that tax direct, of seeing that not one single cent is paid more than the Government gets; that no profits whatever comes upon it; that that system of direct taxation which is to him so dear shall be maintained. But the suggestion is that that shall be all forgotten. Why, he says, there are 50,000 retail merchants who are objecting-and the indirect tax method is to be applied, and not one but two different sets of profits are to be made available on it. The issue is very plain and I do not know that I can usefully say anything more in connection with it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I will take but very few minutes to reply to some of the observations made by the Minister of Finance. It is at any rate quite clear that he persists in his desire to become an unpopular gentleman

in Canada. I want to make my position clear at the outset. I have objected to these taxes because many of them are absolutely unsound. The minister persists in calling them luxury taxes; but they are not luxury taxes at all; for the greater part they are taxes on absolute necessaries of life in this country. If my hon. friend is so desirous of looking after the poor man and the cost of living to the poor man then I would very seriously commend to him that he reconsider this whole tax business and cut out many of the taxes he has imposed on the necessaries of life. My hon. friend states further that one result of the adoption of my amendment will be that retailers will be able to import goods into Canada and thus escape the tax. I think I understood my hon. friend aright; but I cannot for one moment believe that he made that assertion in all seriousness because if he turns to section 7 of the resolution dealing with the one per cent tax that he is imposing under that section, and examines the language, he will find ithat it corresponds identically with the language I have used in my amendment. I was very careful to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman allow me a moment, because'I am quite sure we should not be at cross purposes? It is quite right that the retailer there was not to be taxed; it was only a sales tax.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The amendment states
that the tax shall be paid on importations into the country. Does that mean that a retailer can buy goods in another country and import them into Canada and thus escape the tax? If a retailer goes to the United States and buys a carload of goods for distribution amongst his different stores, does he pay the customs tax? I do not think he escapes that, and if he does not escape the customs tax, how is he going to escape this tax? The idea is absurd, and my hon. friend will realize that if he thinks it over for a moment. My hon. friend made, shall I say, an insinuation, which, I think probably when he considers the matter in the sober light of to-morrow, he will rather regret. He rather hinted that I might be interested in this because I was connected with a certain company that is making importations into this country. I rather regret my hon. friend made that insinuation. I think I am well enough known in this House to have my word accepted when I state that that thought was neveT in my mind for a second.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I gave my hon. friend absolute credit for that. I said that I was sure he had not that thought in mind.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
That furnishes an additional reason why the minister should not have made reference to the matter. But he says further-what good reason is there for changing this? I gave the reasons and I will give them again. If this tax is to be collected by the retailer, it will, in large measure, be evaded. My hon. friend can scarcely get house room enough in Ottawa to house the invoices and returns he is going to compel these retailers to make. If he gets a staff that is adequate to check the returns as they should be checked, a very large proportion of the tax that he will collect will be eaten up with expense. His method is an expensive one and will result in evasion of the tax, as is evident to-day. I have in my desk downstairs a letter which states that already pedlars and vendors of that kind are evading this tax as regards jewellery, drygoods and other commodities. If I had the letter here I would read it. How is my hon. friend going to collect the tax from these people? He is going to hurt the business of the retail merchant in this respect, and his system will inevitably result in evasion of the tax, with a consequent loss of revenue and a great deal of inconvenience to every retail merchant in Canada. I make the appeal to my hon. friend and to the members of the House in the best of good faith, that my hon. friend will find the strongest arguments in support of my amendment came from his own side this afternoon from reputable business men who knew what they were talking about. My hon. friend knows that this tax is an expensive operation and he will not get the revenue he expects) to get from it. For that reason, if for no other, the amendment should be adopted by the committee.
Amendment (Mr. Crerar) negative; yeas, 25; nays, 39.
